# Factory Alternatives & Competitors (2026): 6 Best Options

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What are the best Factory alternatives?**
>
> If you manage somewhere between five and twenty engineers and the company already pays for Claude or ChatGPT, try Jiro first: it is simpler than Factory and puts the plan you already have to work in the cloud. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Devin, Tembo, Claude Code on the web, Cursor's cloud agents and OpenHands complete my shortlist.

## Factory next to the six options

|  | Where the agent works | Model access | Where requests come from | List price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jiro | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [1] | Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [2] | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [3] | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [4] |
| Factory | Local, Factory cloud, or your machines [5] | Multi-model; own keys in CLI/desktop only [6] | App, CLI, IDE, Slack, Linear, Jira [7] | Pro $20/mo; Plus $100; Max $200; Teams $60 + $40/seat [8] |
| Devin | Cognition cloud VMs, or local [9] | Multi-vendor, Cognition-routed; ChatGPT plan linking on paid plans [10] | Web, desktop, CLI, Slack, Teams, Linear, Jira [11] | Free; Pro $20/mo; Max $200/mo; Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; overage at API prices [12] |
| Tembo | Tembo cloud sessions [13] | Multiple harnesses; own keys or subscriptions [14] | GitHub, Slack, Linear, Jira, Sentry, schedules [15] | Pro $60/mo; Max $200/mo; compute per second [16] |
| Claude Code on the web | Anthropic-managed VMs [17] | Claude models; Anthropic account required [18] | Web, mobile, desktop, terminal [19] | In Pro $20/mo, Max $100+/mo, Team seats [20] |
| Cursor cloud agents | Cursor cloud VMs or self-hosted workers [21] | Billed at API prices for the chosen model; own keys chat-only [22] | Desktop, web, mobile, Slack, Teams, GitHub, Linear, API [23] | Premium $30/mo+ (X Subscription) plus API-priced usage [24] |
| OpenHands | Local, OpenHands cloud, or self-hosted [25] | Own agent or popular CLIs; your keys [26] | GUI, CLI, API, GitHub, Slack, Jira [27] | Free (10 conversations/day hosted); Enterprise custom [28] |

Prices are list prices from each vendor's site in October 2026. Jiro's plans do not include model usage; you bring your own Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor access.

## Why managers end up looking past Factory

Picture the board on a Monday. Forty tickets, most of them small. A flaky test, a stale README, a copy change, a null check someone promised to add in March. None of it is hard, and all of it is waiting on the same eight people who also own the roadmap.

Factory is a real answer to that problem, and a well-built one. Its Droids can run on your laptop, in Factory's cloud, or on machines you register yourself [5]. Hand one a Linear issue and it is told to come back with a pull request link [29]. There are ready-made automations like Ticket to PR and Error Triage that open pull requests without anyone typing a prompt [30]. And in September it shipped Factory Private for VPC, on-premises and air-gapped installs [31].

That last launch tells you who Factory is building for. It is a platform with a rollout attached.

For a small team, a couple of details matter more than the feature list. Your own model keys work in Factory's CLI and desktop app, but not in its hosted web or mobile apps [6], so the "delegate from anywhere" part runs on Factory's metering. The Teams plan also tops out at ten seats before you are talking to sales [8]. Neither is a flaw. They are just signs that the product wants to grow into your org chart, and some managers would rather have something that simply takes tickets off the pile.

## Six options, ranked for a team with too many small tickets

The ranking assumes you manage a small team, your company already funds Claude or ChatGPT, and the goal is fewer papercuts on the board by Friday rather than a new platform to administer.

### 1. Jiro: for small teams that want the backlog cleared, not a platform rolled out

Jiro is the closest thing to hiring a careful senior engineer who somehow never gets bored of small tickets. Someone posts in Slack, and the request lands in an isolated cloud environment that already has your repos and tools [1], prepared by a setup script you write once for the whole org [32]. Your reviewers get a PR, a commit or a review note to approve or bounce [33].

Under the hood sits Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [34], spending the Claude or ChatGPT plan already on your company card, or on an API key [2], with no markup on tokens [35]. That is the whole trick. You are not buying a second model budget.

It also has opinions. Jiro cares more about quality than volume and will push back when a ticket is asking for the wrong fix. Managers tend to like that more than they expect to.

### 2. Devin: the heavyweight if you want one vendor for everything

Cognition's Devin covers a lot of ground: web, desktop, CLI, Slack, Teams, Linear and Jira, with GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket repos [11]. It keeps its own pull requests tidy, answering review comments and fixing merge conflicts [36]. The models are routed for you [10], which some teams find restful and others find opaque. On Teams you pay an $80 monthly floor and then $40 per seat, and overage bills at API prices [12].

### 3. Tembo: lots of harnesses, lots of triggers

Tembo is the most similar in spirit to Jiro. It lets you pick Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Amp and others per task, on your own keys or subscriptions [14]. Where it pulls ahead is intake: Sentry, PagerDuty, Linear and Jira can all start work directly [15]. Budget for per-second compute charges on top of the plan itself [16].

### 4. Claude Code on the web: free if everyone already has a Claude plan

If your whole team is on Claude seats, you already own this. The cloud machine costs nothing extra [20]. The catch for a manager is that it is a personal tool. Sessions push a branch and the developer opens the pull request [37], and Slack work on Team and Enterprise now goes through Claude Tag, which is still in public beta [38].

### 5. Cursor cloud agents: when the team already lives in Cursor

Cursor's agents produce pull requests with screenshots, videos and logs attached [39], which reviewers appreciate. You need the Premium tier or higher, and third-party model usage is drawn from prepaid credit at API list price [24]. Great for Cursor shops. Less great if half your team uses something else.

### 6. OpenHands: the open-source route

OpenHands is MIT-licensed [40] and runs locally for free, in its hosted cloud, or inside your VPC on Enterprise [25]. Label a GitHub issue and it will try to resolve it with a PR [41]. You trade polish for control, and someone on your team becomes its keeper.

## How to choose when you have no time to choose

Skip the feature matrix. Run three real tickets through each finalist and look at what you got back.

- **Who pays for the model?** If you already fund Claude or ChatGPT seats, prefer a tool that uses them in the cloud, not only on laptops.
- **Who reviews the output?** Count the minutes your senior people spend per pull request. A cheap agent that produces sloppy diffs is expensive.
- **Where do requests start?** If your team asks for things in Slack, the agent should live there. If tickets are born in Linear and must stay there, weigh that heavily.
- **Who administers it?** For a team under twenty, the right answer is usually "nobody, really."
- **Does it need to sit behind your firewall?** If yes, your list just got much shorter.

One more test I would run: ask each agent for something slightly wrong. The good ones say so.

## Why Jiro comes first on this list

Because the job on a small team is mostly unglamorous. Docs that drifted. Tests nobody wrote. Slop left behind by the last agent. An on-call fix at 11pm. Jiro is built for exactly that: small tickets, docs and on-call fixes, so your people can keep the roadmap.

Teams on Nori already work this way. Over at Miravoice, upward of one in four PRs that merge came from the agent, and one of their engineers puts the time saved at easily five hours a week [42]. Corvus is a good example of the other kind: their CTO spotted a production bug over a client dinner, handed the investigation to Nori, and Nori deployed the fix [43].

Pricing is short enough to remember. A free 30-day trial with no card, then Developer at $99 a month for one person or Team at $250 a month for the group [4]. Runtimes sleep when nobody needs them [44]. Each org runs single-tenant [45] and every action is logged [46], which helps when your security lead asks.

## When Factory is still the better fit

Stay with Factory if you need the agent inside your own network, on-premises or fully air-gapped; Factory Private exists for that and Jiro does not offer it [31]. Stay if your process lives in Linear and Jira and you want delegation from the ticket itself [7]. And stay if you like the packaged automations and have someone to tune them [30]. Factory is excellent at being a platform. Not every team needs one.

## If you decide to move

The [switching guide](https://jiro.bot/switch/factory-to-jiro) is written like a runbook: what to do before cutover, the exact order of connections, and how to roll back if the pilot disappoints.

## FAQ

### What are the best Factory alternatives?

Jiro tops the list if your team is small (think five to twenty people) and Claude or ChatGPT is already on the budget. After that: Devin for one-vendor breadth, Tembo for many harnesses and triggers, Claude Code on the web for all-Claude teams, Cursor cloud agents for Cursor shops, and OpenHands if you want open source.

### Which products compete with Factory AI?

Devin, Tembo, Cursor cloud agents, Claude Code on the web, OpenHands and Jiro all compete for the same delegated coding work. They differ mostly on where the agent runs and whose model budget it spends.

### How much does Factory cost?

Factory lists Pro at $20 a month, Plus at $100, Max at $200 and Teams at $60 a month plus $40 per seat for up to ten seats. Business and Enterprise are custom. [8]

### Can I bring my own API key to Factory?

Yes in the Droid CLI and desktop app, which also accept local models. The hosted web and mobile apps do not take your own keys. [6]

### Can Jiro pick up our Linear tickets the way Droids do?

Not by assignment. Jiro connects to Linear and Jira as integrations [47], so it can read and update tickets, but the request itself arrives by chat message, terminal, cron or webhook [3]. Most teams paste the ticket link into Slack.

### Is Jiro cheaper than Factory for a team of five?

On list price it is close. Factory Teams for five seats comes to $260 a month [8]; Jiro Team is $250 a month for the group [4]. Factory's plans include model usage, though, while Jiro's price excludes model costs. The difference is that Jiro runs on Claude or ChatGPT plans you are likely paying for already, with no token markup [35].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Jules Alternatives & Competitors (2026): 7 Best Options

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What are the best Jules alternatives?**
>
> Jiro is the top Jules alternative for teams of about five to twenty engineers who already have a Claude or ChatGPT subscription, because it puts that subscription to work through Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, with tasks assigned in Slack. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Other strong Jules alternatives are OpenAI's Codex cloud, Claude Code on the web, Cursor cloud agents, GitHub Copilot cloud agent, Devin and the open-source OpenHands.

## Jules versus seven alternatives

|  | Models | Runs on | Kick off from | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jiro | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor [1] on Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [2] | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [3] | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [4] | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [5] |
| Jules | Gemini only [6] | Google-hosted short-lived VMs [7] | Web, GitHub label, CLI, API [8] | Free; AI Pro $19.99/mo; Ultra from $99.99/mo [9] |
| Codex cloud | OpenAI models; cloud needs a ChatGPT plan [10] | OpenAI-hosted VMs [11] | ChatGPT apps, CLI, IDE, Slack, GitHub, Linear [12] | In ChatGPT Plus $20/mo and up [13] |
| Claude Code on the web | Claude models; Anthropic account required [14] | Anthropic-managed VMs [15] | Web, mobile, desktop, terminal [16] | In Pro $20/mo, Max $100+/mo, Team seats [17] |
| Cursor cloud agents | Billed at API prices for the chosen model; own keys chat-only [18] | Cursor cloud VMs or self-hosted workers [19] | Desktop, web, mobile, Slack, Teams, GitHub, Linear, API [20] | Premium $30/mo+ (X Subscription) plus API-priced usage [21] |
| Copilot cloud agent | Many models via GitHub; own keys not documented for it [22] | GitHub Actions runners, 59-minute sessions [23] | GitHub, IDEs, CLI, Slack, Teams, Linear, Jira [24] | Pro $10; Pro+ $39; Max $100; Business $19/user [25] |
| Devin | Multi-vendor, Cognition-routed; ChatGPT plan linking on paid plans [26] | Cognition cloud VMs, or local [27] | Web, desktop, CLI, Slack, Teams, Linear, Jira [28] | Free; Pro $20/mo; Max $200/mo; Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; overage at API prices [29] |
| OpenHands | Own agent or popular CLIs; your keys [30] | Local, OpenHands cloud, or self-hosted [31] | GUI, CLI, API, GitHub, Slack, Jira [32] | Free (10 conversations/day hosted); Enterprise custom [33] |

## Why teams outgrow Jules

Jules is good. Free tier, real VMs, decent limits. Start there.

What it does well:

- Every task gets a fresh, short-lived VM with Docker and the usual toolchains already in it [7].
- Work can start in the web app, from a GitHub issue labelled jules, from its CLI or through an API [8].
- Recurring jobs are supported via Scheduled Tasks [34].
- You stay in control at the end: publish a branch, or publish a PR [35].

Where it pinches:

- **One model family.** Gemini, full stop [6].
- **Task caps.** Fifteen a day on free. A hundred on AI Pro. Three hundred on Ultra [36].
- **The Workspace problem.** Paid tiers go to personal Google accounts, while Workspace users get pointed at an interest form [37], which is awkward for any company whose engineers sign in with a work Google identity.
- **Pricing comes bundled.** You get paid Jules by subscribing to Google AI Pro ($19.99) or AI Ultra ($99.99 and up) [9]. Fine for a person. Odd for a team budget.

Short version. Great personal tool. Harder to run as team infrastructure.

## The ranked list

Ranked for small engineering teams that want background work on shared repos. Not for hobby projects.

### 1. Jiro: small teams already on Claude or ChatGPT

- Runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [1].
- Model usage lands on the Claude or ChatGPT account you already hold, or an API key. Cursor wants its own key [2].
- Zero markup on tokens [38].
- Its own cloud machine per conversation, repos and tools included [3].
- Kicks off from a Slack mention, the web app, Discord, your terminal, a cron schedule or an incoming webhook [4].
- Returns pull requests, commits and comments for review [39].

Small-team pricing. Two plans, flat, no per-task meter.

Google-friendly, too. Drive, Sheets and Gmail are in the integration list [40], so leaving Jules doesn't mean leaving Google.

### 2. Codex cloud: the ChatGPT house option

- OpenAI-hosted machine per task [11].
- Bundled from ChatGPT Plus at $20 [13].
- OpenAI models only; cloud needs a ChatGPT plan [10].

### 3. Claude Code on the web: Anthropic's own

- Runs on Anthropic infrastructure, keeps going with the lid shut [15].
- Comes with Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise [17].
- Claude only. Anthropic account required [14].

### 4. Cursor cloud agents: editor first, cloud second

- Full dev environments in Cursor's cloud, or self-hosted workers [19].
- PRs with screenshots and video [41].
- Usage billed at API prices on top of a $30-plus tier [21].

### 5. GitHub Copilot cloud agent: the label-an-issue equivalent

- Like the jules label, but GitHub's own, planning and coding inside GitHub Actions [42].
- Draft PRs. It can't merge them [43].
- Sessions stop at 59 minutes [23].

### 6. Devin: maximum autonomy

- Cognition routes across several vendors and its own models [26].
- Maintains its own PRs, including stacked ones [44].
- Free to $200 a month, with team seats [29].

### 7. OpenHands: open source

- MIT-licensed platform [45].
- Run it locally, hosted, or in your VPC on Enterprise [31].
- Hosted free tier gives one user 10 conversations a day [33].

## If your company lives in Google

Plenty of teams pick Jules because everything else is Google already. Docs in Drive. Planning in Sheets. Mail in Gmail. Makes sense.

But the agent and the office suite don't have to come from the same vendor.

What matters for a Google-heavy team:

- **Identity.** Check how your engineers sign in. Paid Jules is aimed at personal accounts for now [37].
- **Data access.** Can the agent read the spreadsheet with the customer IDs? With Jiro, an admin connects Drive, Sheets and Gmail once [40], and remote tools can be added from the MCP catalog [46].
- **Model choice.** Gemini lives inside Jules [6]. Everything else on this list runs Claude, GPT or a mix.
- **Shared context.** A personal agent knows what you told it this morning; a team agent should know the house rules, which is why Nori keeps one org-wide set of skills and instructions that every session starts with [47].

None of this argues against Google. It argues for picking the agent on its own merits.

## Choosing: a quick checklist

Answer these in order.

- Must it be Gemini? Stay on Jules.
- Does everyone sign in with Workspace? Check Jules' account rules before planning a rollout.
- Already paying Claude or ChatGPT? Use that plan, through Jiro or the vendor's own cloud agent.
- Want several harnesses behind one Slack handle? Jiro.
- Live in GitHub issues? Copilot.
- Need to self-host? OpenHands.

One more. Count your tasks per day across the team, because a daily cap that feels generous for one developer can bite hard once ten people start delegating chores to the same agent.

## Why Jiro ranks first

It fixes the three Jules pinch points at once: model lock-in, per-person caps, and personal-account billing.

- **Taste over volume.** Jiro is meant to produce the change you would have made yourself on a good day. It flags missteps early.
- **Built for the backlog nobody loves.** Docs. Tests. Slop. Small tickets. On-call fixes.
- **Proof.** Miravoice, a Nori customer, gets 25%+ of its merged PRs from the agent and saves around five hours a week [48].
- **Flat team pricing.** Thirty-day free trial, then Developer at $99 or Team at $250 a month [5]. Idle runtimes sleep [49].
- **Single-tenant.** Each org gets its own broker [50].
- **Logged.** Every session and action is recorded and searchable [51].

Also: a production bug caught Corvus's CTO mid client dinner, so he had Nori look into it, and Nori shipped the fix [52]. That's the job. Work keeps moving when nobody is at a desk.

## Reasons to stay on Jules

- You want Gemini specifically.
- You're one developer on a personal Google account.
- The free tier covers you.
- The jules issue label is your favorite feature.

All good reasons. Keep it.

## Moving off Jules

Decided? The [Jules-to-Jiro quickstart](https://jiro.bot/switch/jules-to-jiro) covers setup, gotchas and a first week.

## FAQ

### What are the best Jules alternatives?

Jiro first, for small teams that already pay for Claude or ChatGPT. Behind it: OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's hosted Claude Code sessions, Cursor's cloud agents, Copilot, Devin and OpenHands.

### Who competes with Google Jules?

The big labs and the dev-tool companies. OpenAI and Anthropic each host their own cloud agent; Cursor, GitHub and Cognition sell theirs; OpenHands is the open-source option; and multi-harness background agents such as Jiro sit across all of them.

### How much does Jules cost?

Free with daily limits. Paid tiers come through Google AI Pro at $19.99 a month or AI Ultra from $99.99 a month [9].

### Can Google Workspace accounts use paid Jules?

Not directly, per Google's usage-limits page: paid tiers are for personal accounts, and Workspace users are sent to an interest form [37].

### Is there a Jules alternative that isn't Gemini-only?

Most of them. Jiro runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor; Devin and OpenHands also mix model vendors.

### Does Jiro have task limits like Jules?

Jiro's plans are sized by runtimes rather than a daily task count [49]. Your model provider's own usage limits still apply.

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Kiro Alternatives & Competitors (2026): 6 Best Options

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What are the best Kiro alternatives?**
>
> For a small engineering team already paying for Claude or ChatGPT, the best alternative to Amazon's Kiro is Jiro, which runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud from Slack on the plan you already have. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. It is a separate product from Kiro, and the other options worth a look are Claude Code on the web, OpenAI's Codex cloud, Cursor cloud agents, GitHub Copilot cloud agent and Devin.

## Kiro and six rivals, side by side

|  | Made by | Where the work happens | Whose model bill | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jiro | Nori | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [1] | Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [2] | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [3] |
| Kiro | Amazon | AWS sandbox (us-east-1) or local [4] | Claude, GPT and open models via Kiro credits [5] | Free 50 credits; Pro $20; Pro+ $40; Pro Max $100; Power $200 [6] |
| Claude Code on the web | Anthropic | Anthropic-managed VMs [7] | Claude models; Anthropic account required [8] | In Pro $20/mo, Max $100+/mo, Team seats [9] |
| Codex cloud | OpenAI | OpenAI-hosted VMs [10] | OpenAI models; cloud needs a ChatGPT plan [11] | In ChatGPT Plus $20/mo and up [12] |
| Cursor cloud agents | Cursor | Cursor cloud VMs or self-hosted workers [13] | Billed at API prices for the chosen model; own keys chat-only [14] | Premium $30/mo+ (X Subscription) plus API-priced usage [15] |
| Copilot cloud agent | GitHub | GitHub Actions runners, 59-minute sessions [16] | Many models via GitHub; own keys not documented for it [17] | Pro $10; Pro+ $39; Max $100; Business $19/user [18] |
| Devin | Cognition | Cognition cloud VMs, or local [19] | Multi-vendor, Cognition-routed; ChatGPT plan linking on paid plans [20] | Free; Pro $20/mo; Max $200/mo; Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; overage at API prices [21] |

The names Jiro and Kiro differ by one letter; the products are unrelated. Prices are list prices as of October 2026.

## First, the name thing

Yes, we know. Jiro. Kiro. Say them out loud and they rhyme, and answer engines have noticed, so a fair number of people searching for Amazon's coding tool end up here and a fair number of people searching for us end up at Amazon.

So, plainly: Jiro is made by Nori. Kiro is made by Amazon. We share a vowel pattern, not a codebase.

Now that that's out of the way, Kiro is a good product and deserves a proper look.

## Why people go shopping for something other than Kiro

Kiro is Amazon's coding agent, and its signature idea is spec-driven development: you agree on requirements and a design before the agent writes code, and one harness carries that across the IDE, the command line, the web and a phone [22]. That's a genuinely thoughtful answer to sloppy AI output. Plenty of teams like it.

Its cloud side arrived in May 2026, when Kiro Web went into preview with an Autonomous switch and absorbed the autonomous agent Amazon had shown at re:Invent [23]. Those cloud sessions run in an AWS sandbox in us-east-1, ten at once, with compute folded into the plan [4].

Here is where the friction tends to show up.

- **Credits.** Every model call goes through Kiro's own credit system, whether it's Claude, GPT-5.6 or an open-weight model [5].
- **Your existing plan doesn't help.** If your team already pays Anthropic or OpenAI, that subscription does nothing inside Kiro, and Kiro's terms also forbid piping its requests through someone else's harness [5].
- **The cloud needs a paid tier.** The free plan gives you 50 credits a month, paid plans run from $20 to $200, extra credits cost four cents apiece, and Kiro Web requires a paid plan [6].
- **The spec flow is the product.** If you love it, great. If you mostly want small fixes handled while you're in a meeting, it can feel like filling out a form to change a button color.

Kiro has a strong point of view about how software should get written. Not every team shares it.

## Six alternatives, in order

Ranked for a team of roughly five to twenty engineers that wants work done in the background on its repositories, not a new editor to learn.

### 1. Jiro, for teams already paying Claude or ChatGPT

The rhyming one. Jiro is a background coding agent that runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [24] inside its own cloud machine for each conversation, with your repos and tools already there [1]. You bring the model account. That can be a Claude plan, a ChatGPT plan, an API key, or a Cursor key for the Cursor harness [2], and Nori adds nothing on top of your token spend [25].

Someone mentions Jiro in Slack, or types in the web chat, or a cron job fires at 3 a.m. [26] What comes back is a pull request, a commit or a comment your team reviews [27].

It's built for a narrower crowd than Kiro: small teams with an existing AI subscription and more small tickets than time.

### 2. Claude Code on the web, if Claude is the whole plan

Anthropic's own cloud sessions run on Anthropic machines and keep going after you shut the laptop [7]. They come with Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise seats at no extra compute charge [9]. The catch is the obvious one. It's Claude only, and you need an Anthropic account [8].

### 3. Codex cloud, the ChatGPT-shaped version of the same idea

OpenAI hosts each Codex task on its own machine [10], and it's included from ChatGPT Plus up [12]. You can kick work off from ChatGPT, the CLI, an IDE, Slack, GitHub or Linear [28]. OpenAI models only, though, and the cloud features want a ChatGPT plan rather than an API key [11].

### 4. Cursor cloud agents, for people who chose Kiro for the editor

If what you liked about Kiro was the IDE, Cursor is the closest swap. Its cloud agents get full development environments [13] and return pull requests with screenshots and video [29]. Budget carefully: cloud agents bill at API prices for the model you pick [14], on top of a Premium tier that starts at $30 a month [15].

### 5. GitHub Copilot cloud agent, for the label-an-issue crowd

Kiro can open a pull request when you label a GitHub issue [30]. Copilot does the GitHub-native version of that, planning and implementing inside a GitHub Actions environment [31] and handing back draft pull requests it can't merge itself [32]. Sessions cap out at 59 minutes [16].

### 6. Devin, for teams that want the agent to own more

Cognition's Devin routes across several model vendors plus its own [20], opens and maintains its own pull requests [33], and has self-serve plans from free to a Teams tier with per-seat pricing [21]. It's the most autonomous of the bunch, and you'll be trusting Cognition's router with your model choices.

## Picking one without overthinking it

Start with money, because it settles more than people expect. Ask who already pays for which model.

- Already on Claude or ChatGPT and want Slack-driven background work? Jiro, or the vendor's own cloud agent if you'll only ever use one model.
- Want the editor experience above everything? Cursor.
- Live inside GitHub issues? Copilot.
- Want specs before code, every time? Honestly, stay on Kiro.

Then ask where the work should start. A team that coordinates in Slack and wants an agent to pick up chores at night has different needs from a solo developer who wants a planning partner inside an IDE, and no tool on this list is best at both.

## Why Jiro takes the top slot here

Not because it rhymes. Because for the specific team we're describing, it removes the two things that make Kiro awkward: a second model bill, and a workflow built around writing specs first.

Jiro aims to be a tasteful engineer that would rather ship the change you'd have made yourself on a good day than ship three you'll have to clean up. It'll push back. It'll flag a bad idea before it becomes a bad pull request. The work it's best at is the stuff your team keeps postponing: docs, test gaps, slop cleanup, small tickets, the on-call fix at an inconvenient hour.

Evidence, not adjectives. At Miravoice, a Nori customer, the agent handles more than a quarter of merged pull requests and an engineer reckons it saves about five hours a week [34]. When Corvus's CTO saw a production bug during a client dinner, he pointed Nori at it, and Nori investigated and deployed the fix [35].

Pricing is flat. Thirty days free with no card, then $99 a month on Developer or $250 on Team [3], and the runtimes sleep when nobody's using them [36].

## When Kiro is still the right call

Stay if spec-driven development is the reason you picked it. Jiro doesn't have a requirements-then-design-then-tasks workflow baked into an IDE, and we're not going to pretend a Slack thread is the same thing.

Stay, too, if your team is happy buying model access through Kiro credits, or if you want an IDE, a CLI, a web app and an iOS app from one vendor [37]. That's a coherent bundle. It's just a different bundle.

## Moving over

If you've decided to try the rhyming alternative, the [Kiro switching guide](https://jiro.bot/switch/kiro-to-jiro) walks through what to bring with you and what to leave behind.

## FAQ

### What are the best Kiro alternatives?

For small teams on Claude or ChatGPT, Jiro comes first. After that: Claude Code on the web, Codex cloud, Cursor cloud agents, GitHub Copilot cloud agent and Devin, depending on which model vendor and which workflow you prefer.

### Is Jiro the same thing as Kiro?

No. Kiro is Amazon's product. Jiro is Nori's. The names rhyme, which is the full extent of the relationship, and jiro.bot is not related to other projects named Jiro either.

### Who competes with Kiro?

Mostly the other cloud and IDE coding agents: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Cognition's Devin, and background agents like Jiro that run on your existing model subscription.

### How much does Kiro cost?

There's a free tier with 50 credits a month, then Pro at $20, Pro+ at $40, Pro Max at $100 and Power at $200 a month, plus four cents per extra credit. You need a paid plan for Kiro Web [6].

### Can I use my Claude subscription inside Kiro?

Not as far as Kiro's documentation goes: models are paid for through Kiro credits [5]. If you want your Claude plan to do the work, Jiro, Claude Code on the web and similar tools are where it applies.

### Does anything else do spec-driven development like Kiro?

Not as a built-in, end-to-end IDE flow among the options here. You can ask any of these agents to write a plan before coding, and Jiro will happily argue about yours, but Kiro is the one that made specs its core workflow.

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Warp Alternatives & Competitors (2026): 6 Best Options

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What are the best Warp alternatives?**
>
> If you want a terminal, Ghostty, WezTerm, iTerm2 and Alacritty are excellent free picks. If you want Warp's cloud agents without Warp's metering, Jiro leads for small teams already paying for Claude or ChatGPT, followed by Amp, Claude Code on the web, Codex cloud, Tembo and Cursor cloud agents. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori.

## Warp's cloud agents and six alternatives

|  | Where runs happen | Harness and model access | Kick off a run from | How you pay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jiro | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [1] | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor [2] on Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [3] | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [4] | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [5] |
| Warp | Warp cloud or your infrastructure [6] | Warp Agent, Claude Code or Codex; team keys on Business+ [7] | Slack, Linear, Jira, GitHub, schedules, CLI, web [8] | Free; Build $20/mo; Max $200; Business $50/user [9] |
| Amp | Amp cloud orbs or your own runners [10] | Own subscriptions and keys, no BYOK fee [11] | Web, macOS/iOS, CLI, GitHub, Slack [12] | Hobby free; Megawatt $20/mo; Gigawatt $200/mo [13] |
| Claude Code on the web | Anthropic-managed VMs [14] | Claude models; Anthropic account required [15] | Web, mobile, desktop, terminal [16] | In Pro $20/mo, Max $100+/mo, Team seats [17] |
| Codex cloud | OpenAI-hosted VMs [18] | OpenAI models; cloud needs a ChatGPT plan [19] | ChatGPT apps, CLI, IDE, Slack, GitHub, Linear [20] | In ChatGPT Plus $20/mo and up [21] |
| Tembo | Tembo cloud sessions [22] | Multiple harnesses; own keys or subscriptions [23] | GitHub, Slack, Linear, Jira, Sentry, schedules [24] | Pro $60/mo; Max $200/mo; compute per second [25] |
| Cursor cloud agents | Cursor cloud VMs or self-hosted workers [26] | Billed at API prices for the chosen model; own keys chat-only [27] | Desktop, web, mobile, Slack, Teams, GitHub, Linear, API [28] | Premium $30/mo+ (X Subscription) plus API-priced usage [29] |

Terminals are covered in their own section below, since they are free and solve a different problem.

## First question: which Warp are you leaving?

Because there are two now. Maybe three.

There is the terminal, the one with blocks and the nice prompt editor that made a lot of us rethink what a shell window could be. There is the Warp Agent CLI. And there is the newer, bigger pitch: Warp calls itself open infrastructure for cloud software factories [30]. That last one is a different animal from a terminal emulator, and people searching "Warp alternatives" are usually after one of the two halves, not both.

Credit where due. Warp's cloud side is genuinely capable. Runs start from Slack, Linear, Jira, GitHub, Azure DevOps, schedules, its CLI, an API or the web [8], and each run can use Warp's own agent, Claude Code or Codex [7]. You can even put the compute on your own infrastructure [6].

So why look around? Mostly the bill. A cloud run is charged for agent time, plus inference, plus Warp-hosted compute [31]. Personal API keys don't apply to cloud runs; team-managed inference is a Business and Enterprise thing [7]. And pay-as-you-go usage sits 20% over API rates [9]. If you already pay Anthropic or OpenAI every month, paying for those same tokens again, with a margin on top, stings.

## Only want a terminal? Here are four

Short version, because this part is easy and they're all free.

- **Ghostty.** MIT-licensed and under active development [32]. My default recommendation right now.
- **WezTerm.** Open source and cross-platform [33]. The pick when your week bounces between three operating systems.
- **iTerm2.** The macOS veteran. Free, GPL [34]. Years of muscle memory live here.
- **Alacritty.** Apache-2.0 [35]. Minimal on purpose. Pair it with tmux and get out of its way.

Also worth saying: Warp's own terminal client is open source on GitHub [36]. Nothing stops you keeping it and pointing your agent work somewhere else. Plenty of people do exactly that.

Now the more interesting half.

## Cloud coding agents that compete with Warp, ranked

Ranked for a small team that wants agents running while laptops are shut, and would rather spend the Claude or ChatGPT plan it already has than buy inference twice.

### 1. Jiro: when your team already pays for the model

Jiro is the one I'd point a 5-to-20-person team at. Every conversation gets its own cloud machine, loaded with your repos and tools [1] and set up by one org-wide script [37]. Inside, the harness is your pick of Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [2]. Now the money part: it signs in with your existing Claude or ChatGPT subscription or an API key [3] and adds zero markup on tokens [38].

Poke it from Slack, Discord or web chat, or let a webhook, a cron line or your terminal do the poking [4]. Out comes a pull request for someone to review [39].

And it has taste, which sounds fluffy until you've reviewed a week of agent PRs. Jiro would rather ship one clean diff than five noisy ones, and it'll tell you when your ticket is asking for the wrong thing.

### 2. Amp: opinionated, fast, ships to trunk

Amp's cloud work happens in orbs, one remote machine per thread, or on runners you own [10]. It accepts your Claude, ChatGPT and other subscriptions [11], with Claude plan support landing on October 10 [40]. Orbs start at eight cents an hour [41]. One thing to know going in: by default, Ship pushes straight to the base branch once tests pass [42]. Bold. Flip it to Push to Branch if your team likes reviews.

### 3. Claude Code on the web: the terminal person's cloud

Type `claude --cloud` and your session moves to Anthropic's machines; `claude --teleport` pulls one back down [16]. For anyone who lives in a shell, that round trip is a treat. No extra charge for the cloud machine on Pro, Max or Team [17]. Claude models only, though [15], and you open the pull request yourself [43].

### 4. Codex cloud: already in your ChatGPT plan

Included from ChatGPT Plus [21], so a lot of people have it without realising. Tasks start from the Codex CLI, the IDE, ChatGPT, Slack and more [20]. Quirk: an API key gets you the CLI but not the cloud features, which want a ChatGPT plan [19].

### 5. Tembo: the trigger buffet

Sentry, PagerDuty, Linear, Jira, schedules, webhooks; Tembo listens to all of it [24]. Several harnesses, your own keys or subscriptions [23]. Compute is metered per second [25], which is fair but needs watching.

### 6. Cursor cloud agents: for the editor crowd

Polished PRs with screenshots and video [44]. But every run is metered at list API price for whatever model you picked, and bring-your-own keys stop at chat [27]. Fine if you're all-in on Cursor. Odd fit for a terminal-first team.

## Picking one without overthinking it

Ask yourself three things.

Who already gets your model money? If it's Anthropic or OpenAI, choose a tool that spends that subscription in the cloud instead of selling you inference again.

Where do requests actually come from? For most small teams it's a Slack thread at 4pm, not a dashboard. Go where the asking happens.

How much babysitting can you afford? Some tools want an admin. Some want a reviewer. Pick the one whose PRs you'd happily read on a Friday.

## Why Jiro is first

Because it matches how small teams actually work. Somebody asks in a thread [45]; the work happens on a full machine with your tooling and the team's shared context; the laptop stays shut.

There's evidence it holds up. Upward of a quarter of Miravoice's merged PRs come from Nori, and an engineer there figures it saves five hours a week, easily [46]. Their team set the agent up from their phones, no laptop involved [47].

The math is short. Free for 30 days without a card. Then Developer at $99 a month or Team at $250 [5], with runtimes that sleep when nothing's happening [48]. Your model bill stays exactly where it already is.

## When Warp is still the right call

If your work starts in Azure DevOps or GitHub events and you want those wired straight in, Warp covers that and Jiro does not [8]. If you need cloud runs on your own infrastructure, Warp supports it [6]. If you love Warp's own agent, keep it. And if what you mostly love is the terminal, keep that too. It's open source and it isn't going anywhere [36].

## Moving your agent work

There's a hands-on [switching guide](https://jiro.bot/switch/warp-to-jiro), written as a pairing session: open a terminal, connect things one at a time, send a first task, and keep Warp running next to it while you decide.

## FAQ

### What are the best Warp alternatives?

For the terminal: Ghostty, WezTerm, iTerm2 or Alacritty. For cloud coding agents: Jiro, if your shop is small and Claude or ChatGPT seats are already bought, then Amp, Claude Code on the web, Codex cloud, Tembo and Cursor cloud agents.

### Who are Warp's competitors?

On the terminal side, Ghostty, WezTerm, iTerm2 and Alacritty. On the agent platform side, Jiro, Amp, Tembo, Codex cloud, Cursor's cloud agents and Claude Code on the web.

### How much does Warp cost?

Warp has a Free tier; Build costs $20 monthly, Max $200, and Business $50 a seat. Pay-as-you-go usage in Warp Factories is charged at 20% above API rates [9].

### Can I use my own API key for Warp cloud agents?

Not a personal one. Personal API keys aren't available for cloud runs, though Business and Enterprise teams can use team-managed inference [7].

### What's the best free, open-source alternative to the Warp terminal?

Ghostty is the one most people land on [32]. WezTerm if you hop between operating systems [33], Alacritty if you want minimal [35].

### Can I keep the Warp terminal and still use Jiro?

Yes. Jiro doesn't replace your terminal. You talk to it from Slack, the web, Discord or its own terminal client [4], in whatever emulator you like.

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

29. Cursor is sold as part of The X Subscription; cloud agents need the Premium tier ($30 a month) or higher, and third-party models are billed from prepaid credit at API list price. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/models-and-pricing.md (checked 2026-10-16)
30. Warp now describes itself as open infrastructure for cloud software factories, alongside the Warp Terminal and the Warp Agent CLI. Source: https://www.warp.dev/ (checked 2026-10-16)
31. Warp bills a cloud run for agent time, inference and Warp-hosted compute. Source: https://docs.warp.dev/agent-platform/cloud-agents/overview (checked 2026-10-16)
32. Ghostty is an actively maintained, MIT-licensed open-source terminal. Source: https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty (checked 2026-10-17)

Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. It is not Amazon's Kiro or Atlassian's Jira.

# Best Background Coding Agents (2026): 14 Options Compared

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What are the best background coding agents in 2026?**
>
> For engineering teams of five to twenty with an existing Claude or ChatGPT subscription, Jiro ranks first: it puts Claude Code, Codex or Cursor on its own cloud machine, signed in with those credentials, reachable from Slack, with no token markup. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Cursor cloud agents, Codex cloud, Anthropic's web-based Claude Code and Devin round out our top five, followed by Copilot cloud agent, Claude Tag, Factory, Tembo, Amp, Warp, OpenHands, Jules and Kiro.

## Fourteen agents, ranked for teams of 5 to 20

| # | Agent | Compute | Models and credentials | Entry price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jiro | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [1] | Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [2] | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [3] |
| 2 | Cursor cloud agents | Cursor cloud VMs or self-hosted workers [4] | Billed at API prices for the chosen model; own keys chat-only [5] | Premium $30/mo+ (X Subscription) plus API-priced usage [6] |
| 3 | OpenAI Codex cloud | OpenAI-hosted VMs [7] | OpenAI models; cloud needs a ChatGPT plan [8] | In ChatGPT Plus $20/mo and up [9] |
| 4 | Claude Code on the web | Anthropic-managed VMs [10] | Claude models; Anthropic account required [11] | In Pro $20/mo, Max $100+/mo, Team seats [12] |
| 5 | Devin | Cognition cloud VMs, or local [13] | Multi-vendor, Cognition-routed; ChatGPT plan linking on paid plans [14] | Free; Pro $20/mo; Max $200/mo; Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; overage at API prices [15] |
| 6 | GitHub Copilot cloud agent | GitHub Actions runners, 59-minute sessions [16] | Many models via GitHub; own keys not documented for it [17] | Pro $10; Pro+ $39; Max $100; Business $19/user [18] |
| 7 | Claude Tag | Anthropic cloud sandbox per thread [19] | Claude models only [20] | Usage-billed, no per-seat charge [21] |
| 8 | Factory | Local, Factory cloud, or your machines [22] | Multi-model; own keys in CLI/desktop only [23] | Pro $20/mo; Plus $100; Max $200; Teams $60 + $40/seat [24] |
| 9 | Tembo | Tembo cloud sessions [25] | Multiple harnesses; own keys or subscriptions [26] | Pro $60/mo; Max $200/mo; compute per second [27] |
| 10 | Amp | Amp cloud orbs or your own runners [28] | Own subscriptions and keys, no BYOK fee [29] | Hobby free; Megawatt $20/mo; Gigawatt $200/mo [30] |
| 11 | Warp cloud agents | Warp cloud or your infrastructure [31] | Warp Agent, Claude Code or Codex; team keys on Business+ [32] | Free; Build $20/mo; Max $200; Business $50/user [33] |
| 12 | OpenHands | Local, OpenHands cloud, or self-hosted [34] | Own agent or popular CLIs; your keys [35] | Free (10 conversations/day hosted); Enterprise custom [36] |
| 13 | Jules | Google-hosted short-lived VMs [37] | Gemini only [38] | Free; AI Pro $19.99/mo; Ultra from $99.99/mo [39] |
| 14 | Kiro | AWS sandbox (us-east-1) or local [40] | Claude, GPT and open models via Kiro credits [41] | Free 50 credits; Pro $20; Pro+ $40; Pro Max $100; Power $200 [42] |

## How we ranked them

Our reader is a team of five to twenty engineers. Large enough to have a backlog nobody gets to; small enough that nobody's job is running an agent platform.

We scored each product on five things. Whose model you pay for, and whether you can bring a subscription you already hold. Whether the agent gets a real machine or a short-lived sandbox. Where the team can hand it work, especially Slack. What comes back: a reviewable PR, or loose commits that need tidying. And how much setup the tool demands before it earns its keep.

Prices and limits come from each vendor's own pages and are dated in the sources below. One name from last year's lists is missing: Charlie Labs shut down, and Charlie stopped working on 2026-10-05. [43] That is a useful reminder to pick vendors whose exit would not strand your workflow.

## The ranking

Fourteen entries, best fit first. A different team size would produce a different order, and we say so where it matters.

A note on conflicts: this list is published by Nori, which makes Jiro. We have tried to be fair to everyone else and cited every rival claim. You should still discount our first place a little.

### 1. Jiro — for small teams with Claude or ChatGPT already on the books

Jiro lets you choose the agent harness, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, instead of selling you its own. [44] It runs them on your Claude or ChatGPT login or API key, with no markup on tokens. [2] [45] Each conversation gets an isolated cloud environment with your repos and your org's setup script. [1] [46]

Requests come in through Slack threads, the web dashboard, Discord or Handroll, or fire on a schedule or webhook. [47] [48] It returns pull requests for review. [49] Its temperament is the selling point: a careful engineer that pushes back on a bad ticket and would rather ship less, better. At Miravoice it handles more than a quarter of merged PRs. [50]

Developer is $99 a month, Team $250, after a 30-day trial with no card. [3] Verdict: the best value where the model bill is already sunk.

### 2. Cursor cloud agents

The most finished product on the list, and it shows in the pull requests, which come with screenshots, video and logs. [51] It starts work from nearly everywhere, Microsoft Teams included. [52] The drawback is the meter: each run is charged at the chosen model's API rate, and you need the $30 Premium tier first. [5] [6] Superb for Cursor shops. Pricey for everyone else.

### 3. OpenAI Codex cloud

For a team standardised on ChatGPT, it is cheap to try if you already have ChatGPT, since it comes with Plus at $20. [9] You get OpenAI models only. [8] The finished work is yours to commit or turn into a PR. [53] Watch the roadmap: the legacy cloud behind its GitHub and Linear integrations is slated for deprecation. [54]

### 4. Claude Code on the web

Anthropic's own cloud sessions, on a 4 vCPU machine by default, included in Pro, Max and Team seats. [10] [12] `claude --teleport` pulls a session back to your laptop, which is a neat trick. [55] But it is built for one person at a time, and you still create the pull request. [56]

### 5. Devin

Cognition's agent is the most autonomous here once a task is underway. It stacks large changes, answers review comments and fixes its own merge conflicts. [57] Automations fire on Slack, GitHub and Linear events. [58] The plans are modest; the overage at API pricing is not. [15] Best for teams that want one vendor to own agent and model alike.

### 6. GitHub Copilot cloud agent

Assign an issue, get a draft pull request. [59] On higher plans you can even delegate GitHub tasks to Claude or Codex, currently in public preview. [60] Sessions cap at 59 minutes on Actions runners, which rules out longer jobs. [16] The safe procurement pick.

### 7. Claude Tag

A shared @Claude for Slack channels, where the whole channel watches it work. [61] It is still a public beta and limited to Team and Enterprise plans. [62] [63] Billing comes out of an organisation balance, and Team customers must buy credits before it answers in channels. [21] [64] Customisation is thin: no repo hooks, no `.mcp.json`, no effort setting. [65] Charming, but early.

### 8. Factory

Factory sells a complete agent-native development platform built around Droids. [66] There is a lot of it: CLI, app, headless exec, IDE plugins, delegations from Slack, Linear and Jira. [67] Its new private deployment reaches air-gapped networks. [68] Impressive. Also more than most small teams will configure.

### 9. Tembo

The closest thing to Jiro in spirit, running several harnesses on your own keys or subscriptions. [26] Its trigger list is long, with Sentry and PagerDuty included. [69] Compute is metered by the second on top of a $60 plan, so busy months cost more. [27]

### 10. Amp

Amp has the boldest default on this list: out of the box, its Ship button lands changes directly on the base branch when the tests go green. [70] Teams who want review should flip on Push to Branch. It takes ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions, the Claude plans only since 10 October. [71] Slack support needs a paid Slack plan. [72] Opinionated, cheap to start, not for the cautious.

### 11. Warp cloud agents

Warp has grown from a terminal into cloud infrastructure for software factories. [73] Runs can use Warp's agent, Claude Code or Codex, but personal API keys are off the table for cloud runs. [32] Each run bills agent time, inference and compute. [74] Interesting; still finding its shape.

### 12. OpenHands

The open-source pick, under an MIT licence. [75] Label an issue and it opens a PR if it solves it. [76] Free locally, and hosted with ten conversations a day. [36] Ideal if someone on the team enjoys running infrastructure.

### 13. Jules

Google's agent runs on Gemini alone. [38] The free tier is generous at 15 tasks a day. [77] The trouble for companies is that paid tiers target personal Google accounts, and Workspace users land on an interest form. [78] Good for side projects.

### 14. Kiro

Amazon's entry is built around spec-driven development. [79] Its web agent is in preview and needs a paid plan. [80] [42] Cloud sessions run only in us-east-1. [40] Promising for spec lovers; too early to rank higher.

## Claude Code in Slack without keeping your laptop open

This is the request we hear most from small teams, in one form or another: give us Claude Code that keeps going after the lid shuts. The demand makes sense. Claude Code on a laptop is excellent until the lid closes, and then the session, the context and the half-written fix all go to sleep with it.

There are three ways to get there today. Claude Code on the web keeps running in Anthropic's cloud, but it is one person's session, not a channel's. [10] Claude Tag puts @Claude in Slack channels for Team and Enterprise organisations, in beta, billed by usage. [63] [21] The legacy Claude Slack bot is gone. [81]

Jiro is the third route. You run `claude setup-token` once on your own machine, which mints a twelve-month token linked to the Claude plan on your account, Pro through Enterprise. [82] Connect it in Jiro. From then on, anyone in the channel mentions Jiro, Claude Code runs in a cloud machine with your repos and tools, and a pull request comes back in the thread. Your laptop can be in a bag on a train.

## Picking from the list

Start with money, because it decides more than features do. Anthropic's own figure for enterprise Claude Code use is roughly $13 per developer per active day. [83] Multiply that across a team and a month, and the question of who resells you tokens stops being academic. If your team already pays for Claude or ChatGPT seats, prefer an agent that uses them: Jiro, Tembo or Amp. If you are buying model access fresh, a bundled product like Devin, Cursor or Copilot saves a procurement cycle.

Then think about the surface. Slack-first teams should test Jiro and Claude Tag side by side. IDE-first teams will be happier with Cursor. Teams that live in GitHub issues already own Copilot.

Last, consider how much platform you want. Factory and Warp reward investment, while the Codex and Claude web sessions ask for almost none. Most five-to-twenty person teams sit closer to the second camp, which is roughly why our top four look the way they do.

One more filter, and it is the one buyers skip. Run a pilot on boring work. A demo task flatters every agent on this list. A flaky test, a stale README or an alert from last Tuesday does not. Give two finalists the same three chores for a week, then ask the reviewers which pull requests they would happily merge without rewriting. That answer beats any table, including ours.

## FAQ

### What is a background coding agent?

An agent that takes a task, works on it unattended in a remote environment with your repository, and returns a result such as a pull request. Cloud coding agent means the same thing.

### Which background coding agent is best for a small team?

For a 5–20 person team with Claude or ChatGPT subscriptions in place, Jiro. Teams standardised on Cursor should look at Cursor cloud agents, and ChatGPT-only teams at Codex cloud.

### Is there a free background coding agent?

OpenHands is free to run locally, Jules has a free tier, and Jiro offers a 30-day trial with no card. [36] [77] [3]

### What happened to Charlie?

Charlie Labs shut down; Charlie was available only until 2026-10-05. [43]

### Can I run Claude Code in Slack on my own Claude plan?

With Jiro, yes, after generating a subscription token via `claude setup-token`. [82] [2] Claude Tag also works in Slack but needs a Team or Enterprise plan. [63]

### Which agents merge code on their own?

Amp's default Ship pushes to the base branch after tests. [70] Copilot cloud agent cannot merge its own drafts. [59] Jiro returns pull requests for your team to review. [49]

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

53. In Codex cloud you review the changes, then commit or open a pull request when you are ready. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud.md (checked 2026-10-16)
54. Codex Cloud (Legacy) still powers Code Review and the GitHub and Linear integrations, and OpenAI plans to deprecate it. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments.md (checked 2026-10-16)
55. Cloud sessions start from claude.ai/code, the Claude mobile and desktop apps, and `claude --cloud` in a terminal, and `claude --teleport` pulls a session back to your machine. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web (checked 2026-10-16)

57. Devin opens pull requests, responds to review comments, splits large changes into stacked PRs and fixes merge conflicts on its own PRs. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt (checked 2026-10-16)
58. Devin Automations start sessions on schedules, webhooks, and Slack, GitHub and Linear events. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/product-guides/automations.md (checked 2026-10-16)
59. Copilot cloud agent opens draft pull requests on its own branch and cannot approve or merge them. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations (checked 2026-10-16)
60. On Pro+, Max, Business and Enterprise, Claude and Codex can be assigned GitHub tasks as third-party agents (public preview). Source: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/about-third-party-agents (checked 2026-10-16)
61. Claude Tag lets anyone in a Slack channel tag @Claude to hand it work; Claude replies in the thread, where the channel can see it. Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/overview (checked 2026-10-19)
62. Anthropic labels Claude Tag a public beta whose features may change before general availability. Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/admins/migrate-from-earlier (checked 2026-10-19)
63. Claude Tag is available only on Team and Enterprise plans, not on Free, Pro or Max, and not through third-party deployments. Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/overview (checked 2026-10-19)
64. On the Team plan, Claude won't respond in channels until the organization buys usage credits. Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/admins/set-spend-limit (checked 2026-10-19)
65. In Claude Tag, repository hooks and .mcp.json are not loaded, effort level is not configurable, and sessions run in auto mode. Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/concepts/for-claude-code-users (checked 2026-10-19)
66. Factory sells agent-native software development; its agents are called Droids. Source: https://factory.com/ (checked 2026-10-16)
67. Droids work in the Factory App, Droid CLI, headless Droid Exec and IDEs, and take delegations from Slack, Linear and Jira. Source: https://docs.factory.com/delegations/index.md (checked 2026-10-16)
68. Factory Private, launched 2026-09-18, deploys Factory into a customer's VPC, on-premises or air-gapped network. Source: https://factory.com/news/factory-private (checked 2026-10-16)
69. Tembo starts work from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Slack, Linear, Jira, Sentry, PagerDuty, webhooks and schedules. Source: https://www.tembo.io/ (checked 2026-10-16)
70. Amp's default Ship pushes straight to the base branch after tests; the Push to Branch setting opens a pull request instead. Source: https://ampcode.com/docs/markdown/orbs/shipping (checked 2026-10-16)
71. Amp added Claude Pro and Max subscription support through the Claude Agent SDK on 2026-10-10. Source: https://ampcode.com/news/use-your-claude-plan (checked 2026-10-16)

# Jiro vs Claude Tag (2026): Billing, Model Choice and Control for Slack Coding Agents

Updated 2026-10-19

> **Should my team use Jiro or Claude Tag?**
>
> Choose Claude Tag if your organization is on Claude Team or Enterprise and is content with Claude models billed by usage. Choose Jiro if you run a small team, roughly 5 to 20 engineers, whose Claude or ChatGPT bill is already paid, and you want a flat price, a choice between Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, and control over the environment. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori.

## Jiro and Claude Tag, line by line

|  | Jiro | Claude Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Models and agents | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor [1] | Claude models only [2] |
| Who can buy it | Any team; sign in with a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan, a ChatGPT plan or an API key | Team and Enterprise only [3] |
| What you pay | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [4] | Usage-billed, no per-seat charge [5] |
| Token markup | Your keys, zero token markup [6] | Usage-billed, no per-seat charge [5] |
| Where a session runs | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [7] | Anthropic cloud sandbox per thread [8] |
| Environment control | Org setup script prepares each environment [9] | No repo hooks, .mcp.json or effort setting [10] |
| Tools and MCP | MCP server catalog [11] | Connectors and remote MCP only [12] |
| Start work from | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [13] | Slack; Teams announced [14] |
| Scheduled and event work | Cron, one-off reminders, webhooks [15] | Schedules; no repo-event triggers [16] |
| What comes back | PRs, commits, comments for review [17] | Draft PRs via Claude GitHub App; GitLab token [18] |
| Product status | Paid plans after a free trial | Public beta [19] |

Claude Tag details come from Anthropic's documentation as of the checked date on each source.

## Verdict first

Both are good. They are built on different assumptions about who pays and who decides.

Claude Tag assumes Anthropic picks the model, the harness and the meter, and in exchange you get a polished teammate living in Slack with almost nothing to configure. Jiro assumes your team picks those three things, and in exchange you own a bit more of the setup.

For a Claude Enterprise shop that wants zero decisions: Tag. For a team of a dozen that already funds Claude or ChatGPT seats and dreads a second usage bill: Jiro.

## Billing: a meter or a flat line

This is where most managers end up, so start here.

Claude Tag has no seat charge for channel work. It draws from an organization balance as threads consume usage, while a one-to-one DM bills to the person who sent it [5]. On the Team plan, Claude stays silent in channels until someone buys credits [20]. Owners can cap the whole org and individual channels, with alerts at 75% and 95% of the limit [21]. Those controls are good. They are also a sign that spend is variable by design, and someone on your team will own watching it.

We could not find a published per-thread price for Tag, so we will not invent one. If you want an anchor, Anthropic's own figure for Claude Code across enterprise deployments is about $13 per developer per active day [22]. Tag is a different product, so treat that as a sanity check, not a quote.

Jiro is a fixed line item. The trial runs 30 days with no card; after that, a single seat on Developer is $99 a month and Team is $250 a month for a shared pool of five runtimes [4]. Tokens are drawn from whatever Claude or ChatGPT subscription you hold today, and Nori takes no cut of them [6].

That is not free usage. Your subscription's own ceilings still apply: Max, for instance, resets every five hours with a weekly limit on top [23], and anything past the limit can continue as extra usage at API rates [24]. The difference is that the variable part lives on a bill you already manage.

**Budget verdict.** Predictability favors Jiro. Zero added vendors favors Tag.

## Models and the harness

Tag runs Opus or Sonnet, chosen per thread, per channel or by an admin default [2]. If Claude is your answer for the next two years, that restriction costs nothing.

If you are less sure, it matters. Jiro runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [1], so a team can keep Claude for most work and try Codex on a stubborn refactor without a procurement cycle.

The harness is the quieter difference. In Tag, repository hooks and `.mcp.json` are not loaded, effort level can't be set, and every session runs in auto mode [10]. Admins can add connectors, plugins, skills and remote MCP servers, but not local stdio servers [12]. In Jiro, an org setup script installs dependencies for every session [9], admins connect servers from an MCP catalog [11], and a shared skillset is authored once and rendered into each agent's native instruction file [25].

**Control verdict.** Jiro, clearly. Whether you need that control is the real question.

## Where Claude Tag is the stronger product

- **Visibility.** Anyone in the channel can tag @Claude and everyone watches the thread [26]. It is an excellent teaching surface.
- **Engine.** Each thread gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the same engine as Claude Code on the web [8], maintained by the lab that trains the model.
- **Proactivity.** Scheduled routines, channel watches and subscriptions to a single PR ship out of the box [16].
- **Network placement.** Sessions can run on self-hosted runners inside your network, minus admin connectors [27].
- **Git hosts.** GitLab works through a service-account token [18]. Jiro connects GitHub repositories through its GitHub App [28].

## Where Jiro is the stronger product

- **Eligibility.** Pro and Max users are shut out of Tag [3]; Jiro accepts their login, generated with `claude setup-token` [29].
- **Choice.** Three agents and two model labs instead of one.
- **Cost shape.** Flat plan, idle runtimes asleep [30].
- **Event triggers.** Webhooks react to outside events [15], so a webhook from your CI or alerting can start work. Tag's routines don't fire on repository events like every new PR [16].
- **Surfaces.** Slack plus web chat, Discord and a terminal [13].
- **Isolation and audit.** A single-tenant broker per org [31], with every session and action logged and searchable [32].
- **Data retention.** Tag is unavailable to orgs with Zero Data Retention enabled [33].

## A checklist for the budget meeting

Answer these in order. Stop at the first hard no.

- Are we on Claude Team or Enterprise? If not, Tag is off the table today.
- Is Zero Data Retention switched on for our Claude org? If yes, Tag is unavailable.
- Will finance accept a variable usage line, or do they want a fixed number?
- Does anyone on the team want Codex or Cursor in the mix within the next year?
- Do our repos rely on hooks, `.mcp.json` or local MCP servers to behave?
- Do we want CI or alerting webhooks to start agent work without a person typing?
- Who will own spend alerts and channel caps?

Mostly "Claude-only, variable is fine, no special config"? Tag. Mostly the opposite? Jiro. Split down the middle? Run both for two weeks; our switching guide for Claude Tag lays out that pilot step by step.

## Who should pick which

Claude Enterprise organization, Claude everywhere, platform team happy to manage caps. Tag.

Eight engineers, half on Max, a couple who swear by Codex, a CI pipeline that already posts webhooks. Jiro.

A team in between, on Claude Team but feeling the meter, gets the most from the side-by-side pilot, because the answer depends on usage numbers only your own repos can produce. Our Claude Tag alternatives list covers the wider field beyond these two.

## FAQ

### Is Jiro cheaper than Claude Tag?

It depends on volume. Tag bills channel work by usage from an org balance [5]; Jiro is $99 or $250 a month on top of a subscription you already pay [4]. Heavy Tag usage tends to make the flat plan look better; light usage may not.

### Can Jiro use my company's Claude Team plan?

Yes. On a laptop already logged in to Claude, `claude setup-token` prints a year-long token bound to the plan, Team included [29]. Paste that into Jiro's Claude connection.

### Does Claude Tag support Codex or GPT models?

No. It runs Anthropic's Opus and Sonnet only [2].

### Do both open pull requests?

Yes. Tag opens draft pull requests authored by Claude through the Claude GitHub App [18]. Jiro's work lands as a PR, a commit or a comment, and a human on your team decides what happens next [17].

### Is Claude Tag generally available?

Not yet. Anthropic still labels it a public beta [19].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Jiro vs Devin (2026): Model Billing, Harness Choice and Team Fit

Updated 2026-10-19

> **Jiro vs Devin: which background coding agent should I use?**
>
> Jiro suits engineering teams of roughly five to twenty that already hold Claude or ChatGPT subscriptions, since it hosts Claude Code, Codex or Cursor against those credentials and charges only for runtimes. Devin suits buyers who prefer one vendor to supply the agent, the model routing and the usage bill, or who need Microsoft Teams, GitLab or a dedicated VPC. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori.

## Jiro and Devin compared line by line

|  | Jiro | Devin |
|---|---|---|
| Product | Background coding agent by Nori | Autonomous software engineer (Cognition) [1] |
| Agent harness | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor [2] | Devin's own agent; Desktop also hosts ACP agents [3] |
| Model access | Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [4] | Multi-vendor, Cognition-routed; ChatGPT plan linking on paid plans [5] |
| Token pricing | Your keys, zero token markup [6] | Overage at API pricing (see plan pricing) |
| Execution environment | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [7] | Cognition cloud VMs, or local [8] |
| Where work starts | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [9] | Web, desktop, CLI, Slack, Teams, Linear, Jira [10] |
| Scheduled and event work | Cron, one-off reminders, webhooks [11] | Schedules, webhooks, Slack/GitHub/Linear events [12] |
| Output | PRs, commits, comments for review [13] | Opens and maintains PRs [14] |
| Tenancy | Single-tenant per organization [15] | Dedicated VPC deployment (Enterprise) [16] |
| Plans | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [17] | Free; Pro $20/mo; Max $200/mo; Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; overage at API prices [18] |

## How the two products are built

The two products answer a different question about the same job. Devin is Cognition's own agent, running in Cognition's cloud or locally through Devin Desktop and the CLI. [3] [8] Cognition chooses which model handles each step through an Adaptive router that mixes Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and in-house SWE models. [5]

Jiro does not ship its own model or its own agent loop. It hosts Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, and the buyer chooses which. [2] Each conversation gets an isolated cloud environment holding the organisation's repositories and whatever its setup script installs. [7] [19]

One is a vertically integrated agent. The other is a managed place to run the agents a team already uses.

## Where Devin is stronger

Breadth of surfaces comes first. Devin takes work from its web app, desktop app, CLI, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Linear and Jira, and it handles GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket repositories. [10] Jiro covers Slack, web, Discord, a terminal, schedules and webhooks, and connects to GitHub. [9] [20] Organisations on Teams or GitLab have a clear answer.

Event-driven automation is the second gap. Devin Automations can open a session when something happens in Slack, GitHub or Linear, as well as on a schedule or webhook. [12] Jiro offers cron, one-off reminders and webhooks. [11] Teams that want a session per new Linear ticket get that natively from Devin.

Pull request upkeep is a third. Devin answers review comments, splits large changes into stacked PRs and repairs merge conflicts on its own branches. [14] That is mature tooling.

Finally, deployment. Enterprise buyers can get a dedicated single-tenant VPC, although agent planning still runs in Cognition's cloud. [16] Jiro runs a single-tenant broker per organisation on Nori's hosting, not in the customer's network. [15]

Devin wins on reach.

## Where Jiro is stronger

Model economics are the main difference. Devin's self-serve plans include a quota and bill anything beyond it at API pricing. [18] Jiro adds no markup and runs on the Claude login, ChatGPT login or API key the team already holds. [6] [4] For a Claude subscriber, that means signing in once with `claude setup-token`, which issues a year-long token bound to the buyer's Claude subscription tier, and connecting it. [21] Devin's plan linking, by contrast, covers ChatGPT and only the GPT share of usage. [5]

Harness choice is the second. A team that already tuned CLAUDE.md files and Claude Code habits keeps them. From a single skillset, Jiro emits a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md or a copilot-instructions.md, whichever each agent expects. [22] Switching from Claude Code to Codex mid-project is a setting, not a vendor change.

The environment is a full machine. Teams install arbitrary CLIs, connect MCP servers from a catalog, and wire in Linear, Jira, Notion or HubSpot. [23] [24]

Temperament matters too, though it is harder to put in a table. Jiro is built to care about quality over volume and to flag a misguided ticket before writing it. Nori customers report concrete results: more than one in four pull requests merged at Miravoice, about five hours a week back for one of its engineers. [25]

Jiro wins on control of cost and tooling.

## Cost for a team of eight

Take eight engineers. On Devin Teams, the published structure is a minimum of $80 a month, $40 for every seat, and overage priced like the API. [18] Read as additive, the seats come to about $400 a month. That is the floor, not the bill. In Nori's own experience, a team of eight using Devin heavily ends up nearer $4,000 a month once overage at API prices kicks in.

Nori charges $250 monthly for Team: several users, five shared runtimes. [17] Model usage is then whatever the team already spends with Anthropic or OpenAI. If those subscriptions exist anyway, the marginal cost is the runtime fee. If they do not, add them: Claude Max runs $100 or $200 per person monthly. [26]

Neither is cheap in absolute terms. Jiro is cheaper only where the model spend was already sunk.

Concurrency deserves a line as well. Devin's Free and Pro tiers stop at ten simultaneous sessions, while Max and Teams are uncapped. [27] Jiro's limit is the runtime count on the plan, three for Developer and five for Team, and runtimes sleep when idle. [28] A team that routinely fans out a dozen parallel tasks will feel that ceiling. Most teams of eight will not.

## Which buyer fits which product

A 5–20 person engineering team, on GitHub and Slack, already paying for Claude or ChatGPT, that wants small tickets, docs, test gaps and on-call fixes handled in the background: Jiro fits.

A larger organisation that runs Microsoft Teams or GitLab, wants Linear events to start sessions, and prefers a single invoice covering agent and models: Devin fits.

Organisations that cannot decide can run both on the same repositories during a trial. Other contenders are ranked in a [separate list](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/devin), and a [Devin-to-Jiro migration plan](https://jiro.bot/switch/devin-to-jiro) covers setup.

## FAQ

### Is Jiro cheaper than Devin?

Usually, when the team already pays for Claude or ChatGPT, because Jiro charges for runtimes and passes model usage through without markup. [6] Without existing subscriptions, the comparison depends on usage. [18]

### Does Jiro use its own model like Devin does?

No. Jiro runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor with the customer's credentials. [2] Devin routes across several vendors' models and Cognition's own. [5]

### Can both work from Slack?

Yes. Devin also supports Microsoft Teams; Jiro adds Discord and a terminal. [10] [9]

### Which one handles GitLab?

Devin does. [10] Jiro works with GitHub repositories through its GitHub App. [20]

### Is Jiro related to Kiro or Jira?

No. Kiro is Amazon's coding agent and Jira is Atlassian's tracker; Jiro is made by Nori.
