# Jiro vs Kiro (2026): Two Different Coding Agents, Explained Simply

Updated 2026-10-19

> **What is the difference between Jiro and Kiro?**
>
> Jiro and Kiro are two separate products from two separate companies: Kiro is Amazon's spec-driven coding agent, and Jiro is Nori's agent that takes jobs from Slack and runs them in the cloud on a Claude or ChatGPT plan your team already owns. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Kiro suits developers who want to plan in detail inside an IDE; Jiro suits small engineering teams that want routine work handed off and returned as pull requests.

## Jiro and Kiro, row by row

|  | Jiro | Kiro |
|---|---|---|
| Company | Nori | Amazon |
| What it is | Background coding agent your team messages | Amazon's spec-driven coding agent [1] |
| Where it works | Isolated cloud environment with your repos and tools [2] | AWS sandbox (us-east-1) or local [3] |
| Where you talk to it | Slack, web, Discord, terminal, schedules, webhooks [4] | IDE, CLI, web, iOS; GitHub and GitLab [5] |
| How AI usage is paid for | Your Claude/ChatGPT login or API key; Cursor key [6]; Your keys, zero token markup [7] | Claude, GPT and open models via Kiro credits [8] |
| Monthly price | Free 30-day trial; Developer $99/mo; Team $250/mo [9] | Free 50 credits; Pro $20; Pro+ $40; Pro Max $100; Power $200 [10] |
| What you get back | PRs, commits, comments for review [11] | Opens PRs; never auto-merges [12] |

Prices as of October 2026. Jiro's price does not include your Claude or ChatGPT plan.

## Are Jiro and Kiro the same company?

No. This is the most common mix-up, so it comes first.

Kiro belongs to Amazon. Jiro belongs to Nori, a much smaller company. The names sound alike by accident. There is no partnership, no shared technology, and no shared account between them.

If you were looking for Amazon's product, you want kiro.dev. If you were looking for us, you're in the right place.

## What does Kiro do, in plain terms?

Kiro is a tool that helps developers write software with AI. Its big idea is called spec-driven development. Before any code gets written, you and the AI agree on a written plan for what to build and how [1].

Think of it like an architect drawing blueprints before the builders arrive.

Developers can use it inside a code editor, at the command line, in a web browser or on an iPhone [5]. Since May 2026 there is also a web version that can work on its own in the background, though it is still labelled a preview [13].

## What does Jiro do, in plain terms?

Jiro is closer to a colleague you can send a message to. Someone on your team writes "@Jiro please fix the broken signup email" in Slack, and Jiro goes off and does it.

It works on its own computer in the cloud, which already has your company's code and tools set up [2]. When it's done, it sends back a pull request. That is simply a proposed change that a person on your team reads and approves before it goes live [11].

Nobody has to keep a laptop open. Jiro can also run on a schedule, say every Monday morning, or when another system pings it [14].

## How is paying for each one different?

This is the part buyers usually care about most.

With Kiro, you buy a Kiro plan, and AI usage comes out of Kiro's own credits [8]. Plans go from free, with 50 credits, up to $200 a month, and the background web version needs a paid plan [10].

With Jiro, you pay Nori a flat monthly fee, and the AI itself runs on an account you probably already have with Anthropic (Claude) or OpenAI (ChatGPT) [6]. Nori doesn't add a markup to that usage [7]. The fee is $99 a month for one person or $250 a month for a team, after a 30-day free trial that doesn't ask for a card [9].

So which is cheaper? For one developer who just wants an AI helper in their editor, Kiro's $20 Pro plan will usually cost less than Jiro plus a Claude subscription. For a team of ten that already pays for Claude, adding Jiro can be cheaper than buying everyone a second AI plan, because you aren't paying for the same models twice.

## Which one is better at what?

Kiro is stronger when:

- the work is large and needs careful planning first;
- a developer wants to stay inside a code editor all day;
- you'd rather buy AI usage from one place and not manage separate model accounts.

Jiro is stronger when:

- the work is a steady stream of small jobs, like fixing bugs, writing docs or filling in missing tests;
- your team already talks in Slack and wants to hand work off there;
- you already pay for Claude or ChatGPT and want to use that plan rather than buy credits elsewhere;
- you want to switch between Claude Code, Codex and Cursor without changing tools [15].

## Who should buy which?

Pick Kiro if you are a developer, or a team of developers, who wants a structured planning process built into the tools you code in, and you're comfortable with Amazon as the vendor.

Pick Jiro if you lead a small engineering group, roughly five to twenty people, that already pays for Claude or ChatGPT and keeps running out of hours for the small stuff.

A real example helps here. At Miravoice, a Nori customer, the agent now produces over a quarter of the pull requests that get merged [16]. They got it running from their phones [17].

## FAQ

### Is Jiro made by Amazon?

No. Kiro is made by Amazon. Jiro is made by Nori. This site also has no connection to any other software that happens to be called Jiro.

### Is Jiro a version of Kiro, or the other way around?

Neither. They were built separately, they work differently, and you'd sign up for each one on its own.

### What is a background coding agent?

It's an AI helper that works on code while you do something else. You describe the job, it goes away and does it on a computer in the cloud, and later you get back a finished change to check. Jiro works this way, and Kiro Web added a similar background mode in 2026 [13].

### Which AI models can each one use?

Kiro offers Claude, GPT-5.6 and some open models, all paid through Kiro [8]. Jiro runs three popular coding tools, Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, which use Anthropic, OpenAI and Cursor accounts respectively [15].

### Can I use both at the same time?

Yes. Some developers could plan bigger features in Kiro and let Jiro pick up small tickets from Slack. They don't share accounts or settings, so you'd set each up separately.

### Do I need to be technical to use Jiro?

Someone technical should do the initial setup, which means connecting your GitHub code and your AI account. After that, anyone on the team can ask for work in plain English in Slack, and an engineer reviews the result before it ships.

### Does Kiro let me use my existing Claude subscription?

Kiro sells model access through its own credits, and its terms don't allow sending its requests through other tools [8]. Jiro is built the other way round: your Claude or ChatGPT plan is the engine.

### Which is safer for company code?

Both open proposed changes for a human to review rather than shipping straight to production; Kiro, for example, won't merge its own changes [12]. Jiro gives each company its own separate setup [18] and keeps a log of every action it takes [19].

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Amp to Jiro (2026): Checklist, Gotchas and a Review-First Setup

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Amp to Jiro?**
>
> Keep your AGENTS.md in the repo, start a Jiro trial, install the GitHub App on the repos you want, connect Slack, then link your Claude plan with `claude setup-token` or your ChatGPT plan with Codex OAuth. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Before the first task, turn on branch protection, because Jiro hands work back as pull requests for review rather than pushing to your base branch.

## Before you touch anything

Read this list once. Then start.

- **Gotcha:** Out of the box, a green test run in Amp is followed by Ship landing the change on your base branch [1]. Your team may have grown used to changes simply appearing on main. In Jiro they arrive as pull requests, so somebody has to own review from day one.
- **Gotcha:** Claude plan access does not transfer between tools. Amp reaches your Claude Pro or Max plan through the Agent SDK [2]; Jiro needs its own token, generated on your laptop.
- **Gotcha:** if any Amp threads are still running in orbs, let them finish or ship them first. They will not migrate.
- Pick one or two repositories for the pilot. Not all of them.

## What comes with you

Your AGENTS.md comes along for free. It lives in the repository, not in Amp, so Jiro sees it on the first clone; Codex reads it as-is.

Team-wide rules you want everywhere, across repos, belong in a Jiro skillset instead. You write a skillset one time; Jiro renders it into whatever file each harness expects: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for most others [3]. Move anything that used to live only in someone's Amp thread history by hand. Nothing imports it automatically, and we would rather say so now.

Want Jiro's engineering habits in your own repos too? `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` adds them.

## Setup, step by step

- **Step 1: Open a trial account.** It runs a month and asks for no payment details [4].
- **Step 2: Install the GitHub App.** Choose every repository or just the pilot set [5]. Choose the pilot set.
- **Step 3: Protect the branch.** In GitHub, require a pull request and at least one approving review on main for each pilot repo. Do this before step 6. Seriously.
- **Step 4: Connect Slack.** Requests and replies then sit in threads your whole team can read [6] [7].
- **Step 5: Connect a model.** For Claude, open a terminal on your own machine and run `claude setup-token`. Out comes a token good for twelve months and bound to the Claude subscription you already pay for, be it Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise [8]. Copy it into Jiro. For ChatGPT, sign in through Codex OAuth or add an OpenAI API key; Cursor takes a Cursor API key [9].
- **Step 6: Write the org setup script.** Install runtimes, dependencies and CLIs once, and every session's environment starts ready [10].
- **Step 7: Hand over a first task.** Something small and verifiable, posted in a Slack thread.

**Gotcha:** run step 5 on your own computer, not inside Jiro. The token exists for machines that cannot open a browser login, and Jiro's cloud environments are exactly that kind of machine.

## Set up the review flow properly

This is the part teams skip. Do not skip it.

Decide who reviews agent pull requests, and say so in the repo's CODEOWNERS file if you use one. Agree on what earns an approve versus a request for changes. Then tell Jiro, in the skillset, what your reviewers care about: test coverage on touched code, naming, no drive-by refactors. It flags missteps early and will push back on a vague ticket, which works best when reviewers and agent share the same bar.

One more thing. Reply to its pull requests the way you would reply to a colleague's. Specific comments get specific fixes.

## A first week that tells you something

- **Monday:** ask Jiro to read one pilot repo and propose three improvements it would make first. Judge its taste before its speed.
- **Tuesday:** a documentation pass on the module nobody wants to explain.
- **Wednesday:** fill test gaps around a recently changed file.
- **Thursday:** clean up slop, such as dead flags, duplicated helpers or copy-pasted error handling.
- **Friday:** one small ticket from the backlog, plus a scheduled job for next week [11].

If something breaks in production that week, try the on-call fix from Slack. That is where background agents earn their keep.

## What you give up

Be honest with yourself about these.

- Native macOS and iOS apps and an SDK [12]. In Jiro you work from Slack, Discord, the browser or a terminal, and timers or webhooks can kick things off too [6].
- Choosing a machine size per thread and paying for it by the minute [13].
- A free tier for keeps. Amp's Hobby plan stays free with your own runners [14]; Jiro's trial ends after thirty days.
- Ship-to-main convenience. You traded it for review on purpose.

## Cost check

Amp: Hobby free, Megawatt $20 and Gigawatt $200 a month, plus orb minutes where the plan does not cover them [14] [13].

Jiro: $99 a month on Developer for a single engineer and up to three persistent runtimes; $250 a month on Team for several people sharing five [4]. Runtimes sleep when idle [15], and your Claude or ChatGPT bill is unchanged, because Jiro takes no cut of tokens [16].

**Gotcha:** for a single developer on Megawatt, Jiro costs more. The case for paying it is shared runtimes, Slack threads the whole team sees and work that comes back as a pull request for review, not a lower invoice.

## Running both during the pilot

Nothing stops you keeping Amp for a few weeks. Split work by repository, never by task, so two agents are not editing the same branch. Turn on Push to Branch in Amp for the overlap period [1], which puts both tools behind the same review gate and makes the comparison fair.

Compare merged pull requests, review rounds per change and how often a reviewer had to rewrite something. Ignore raw volume.

Still deciding? The [Amp alternatives comparison](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/amp) lays out the other options.

## FAQ

### Will my AGENTS.md work in Jiro?

Yes. It stays in the repository, so Jiro picks it up on clone. Rules shared across repos can go into a skillset, which Jiro translates into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md per harness [3].

### Can I use the same Claude Max plan I used with Amp?

Yes, with a new token. Run `claude setup-token` locally [8] and connect the result in Jiro.

### Does Jiro land changes on main like Amp's Ship?

Jiro's normal output is a pull request (sometimes a commit or comment) that your team reviews [17]. Enforce that with GitHub branch protection on main, so changes only land through review.

### Is our code kept apart from other Jiro customers?

Each organization runs on its own single-tenant broker [18], one machine serves one active session [19], and every action is logged [20].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

13. Orbs are billed per minute, from $0.08 an hour for the smallest size. Source: https://ampcode.com/docs/markdown/orbs/sizes-and-costs (checked 2026-10-16)
14. Amp's Hobby tier is free with pay-as-you-go orbs or your own runners; Megawatt is $20 a month and Gigawatt $200 a month with included orb time and agent usage. Source: https://ampcode.com/pricing (checked 2026-10-16)
15. Nori sizes plans by runtimes, which sleep when idle and wake on demand; the trial runs five for 30 days. Source: https://noriagentic.com/#faq (checked 2026-10-19)
16. Nori's comparison table lists any model on your own keys with flat pricing and zero token markup. Source: https://noriagentic.com/#compare (checked 2026-10-19)
17. Nori agents can return a pull request, commit, comment or completed task for you to review, merge or send back. Source: https://noriagentic.com/#faq (checked 2026-10-19)
18. Each hosted Nori organization gets a single-tenant broker on its own subdomain. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/sessions/concepts/security-and-credentials#organization-isolation (checked 2026-10-19)
19. In Nori, one claimed machine serves one active session within the organization's fleet. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/resources/faq#is-each-session-isolated (checked 2026-10-19)
20. Nori logs every session and every action, and makes them searchable. Source: https://noriagentic.com/for-security-leaders.html (checked 2026-10-19)

# Switching from Claude Code on the Web to Jiro (2026): A Note to the Team

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Claude Code on the web to Jiro?**
>
> Keep your Claude plan and your repo's CLAUDE.md; both come with you. Run `claude setup-token` on your own machine, connect that token in Jiro, install the GitHub App, add Jiro to Slack and write a short setup script, then hand it a small task. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. It's meant for small teams whose Claude or ChatGPT plans are already paid for.

## Hey, quick note before we move anything

Hey all. Here's how we move our Claude Code work into Jiro, and why it shouldn't hurt.

Short version: nothing we like about Claude Code goes away. Jiro runs Claude Code itself [1], on the same Claude subscriptions we already pay for. What changes is where the work lives. Instead of each of us kicking off cloud sessions from our own claude.ai account, the whole team asks Jiro in Slack, and the work happens on a cloud machine with our repos and tools already set up [2].

Basically: our Claude Code, minus the open laptop. Anyone's laptop.

## What comes with us

More than you'd think.

- **Our CLAUDE.md.** It's committed in the repo, so it's there on every task. No copying.
- **Your personal CLAUDE.md** (the one in your home folder). That one stays on your laptop. If there's something in it the whole team should follow, paste it into our shared skillset. Nori turns one skillset into each agent's file, CLAUDE.md for Claude Code included [3].
- **Your Claude plan.** Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise all work through a setup token [4]. More on that below.
- **The repos.** Same GitHub org. We just install a different GitHub App and pick which repos it sees [5].
- **The environment setup** we each fiddled with for cloud sessions. That becomes one org setup script that every session runs [6]. Write it once, done.
- **Tools we already wired up.** Linear, Jira, Notion and friends connect through the integrations page [7]; MCP servers come from the catalog [8].

## Setting it up

I'll do steps 1 to 3 and 5. Everyone does step 4 for themselves, with their own token. No shared logins.

- **1. Start the trial.** It's free for a month, and nobody asks for a card [9].
- **2. Hook up GitHub.** Install Jiro's GitHub App and tick the repos. I'll start with the API and the web app, nothing else.
- **3. Add Jiro to Slack.** It'll join the eng channel first.
- **4. Sign in with Claude.** Open a terminal on your laptop and type `claude setup-token`. You get back a token that's good for a year on your plan [4]. Paste it into Jiro's Claude connection. Prefer Codex? OAuth or an OpenAI key works too; Cursor wants its own Cursor key [10].
- **5. Write the setup script.** Node, our Postgres fixtures, the CLI we keep forgetting to install.
- **6. Try one small thing.** Ask Jiro to fix a typo in the README. If a pull request shows up and CI goes green [11], we're live.

Bonus round: want Jiro's engineering habits inside the Claude Code on your laptop? Paste `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` into a terminal.

## What I'd like us to try in week one

Boring stuff first. On purpose.

- The docs nobody has updated since the auth rewrite.
- Tests for the billing module, which has none. Yes, none.
- That pile of AI-generated helpers from last quarter that sort of duplicate each other. Let's clean them up.
- Three or four small tickets from the backlog that keep getting bumped.
- One on-call fix. If something pages us this week, let's ask Jiro first and see what it does.
- A weekly cron job that checks for stale TODOs and opens a PR [12].

Jiro is pretty opinionated. It'll push back if a plan looks off, and it'll flag stuff early. Don't take it personally. It does it to me too.

## What we give up

I want to be honest about this part.

- **Teleport.** Pulling a cloud session back to your terminal with `--teleport` is a Claude Code on the web thing [13]. Jiro work comes back as a PR instead.
- **The Claude apps.** Starting a cloud session from the Claude mobile or desktop app goes away for team work. Jiro's web chat and Slack work fine on a phone; Miravoice set their whole agent up that way [14].
- **Free cloud machines.** Anthropic includes the cloud VM in our plans [15]. Jiro's plan is a separate line.
- **Auto-fix after the PR.** Cloud sessions can push fixes for CI failures and review comments on their own [16]. With Jiro, we ask in the thread [17].
- **One vendor.** Now there are two.

If any of those is a dealbreaker for you personally, keep using claude.ai/code for your solo stuff. Nobody's taking it away.

## What it costs us

Our Claude plans stay as they are: Pro is $20 a month and Max starts at $100 [15]. Jiro sits on top. For the team, that's the Team plan at $250 a month, five runtimes we all share; Developer is $99 if it's just one person [9]. The runtimes sleep when nobody's using them [18].

Nori doesn't mark up tokens [19], so the model bill is still just our Claude bill. If someone burns through their Max limit, extra usage bills at API rates, same as today [20].

So yes, it's an extra $250. What we're buying is that the PM, the on-call person and the new hire can all start real work without a laptop session of their own.

## Running both for a bit

For the first two weeks, nothing gets switched off. Use Jiro for team work in Slack, keep claude.ai/code for whatever you do alone. At the end we'll look at what got merged and decide.

If you want to see how Jiro stacks up against the other options first, the [list of Claude Code on the web alternatives](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/claude-code-web) is a decent read. Questions? Reply in the thread.

## FAQ

### Does my CLAUDE.md work in Jiro?

Yes. A CLAUDE.md committed to the repo is part of the code Jiro checks out, and Jiro runs Claude Code, which reads it.

### Do I need an Anthropic API key, or can I use my Claude subscription?

Your subscription is fine. From a terminal on your laptop, `claude setup-token` creates the token you connect [4]. An API key also works [10].

### Can I keep using Claude Code on the web after switching?

Yes. Your Claude plan is unchanged, so claude.ai/code keeps working for solo sessions.

### What happened to the Claude Code app for Slack?

Anthropic shut the old bot down on October 5, 2026. For Team and Enterprise orgs, Slack requests are Claude Tag's job now [21].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Claude Tag to Jiro (2026): A Two-Week Side-by-Side Pilot

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Claude Tag to Jiro?**
>
> Do not cut over in one step. Keep Claude Tag in its current channels, stand Jiro up in a neighboring channel on the Claude or ChatGPT login the team already pays for, route comparable tasks to each for two weeks, and decide from recorded results. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Its target is small teams of roughly 5 to 20 engineers on Claude or ChatGPT.

## Pilot scope

Duration: 14 calendar days. Participants: three to six engineers, one of whom acts as pilot lead. Channels: the existing Claude Tag channel stays untouched; one new channel is created for Jiro.

Objective: establish, with numbers, whether Jiro produces mergeable work at a predictable cost for this team's repositories. Not whether it is impressive in a demo. Demos are cheap.

Exit criteria are fixed before day one and written into the channel topic. A reasonable default: Jiro is adopted if its merge rate is at least equal to Claude Tag's on comparable tasks and the total monthly cost is lower or flat.

## What carries over, and what has to be rebuilt

Most of a Claude Tag setup lives in three places: the repository, Anthropic's admin console and Slack. Each moves differently.

- **Repository CLAUDE.md files.** These travel with the code. Jiro runs Claude Code [1] against a clone of the repo, so committed instructions are present on the first task.
- **Skills added in the Tag admin console.** Copy them by hand into an org skillset. Nori converts the skillset into the instruction-file format each harness expects [2].
- **Connectors, plugins and remote MCP servers.** Reconnect each from Jiro's integrations page or MCP catalog [3]. Linear, Jira, Notion and Google are among the listed integrations [4].
- **Scheduled routines.** Recreate them as cron triggers [5].
- **Channel watches and single-PR subscriptions.** No direct equivalent is documented. Where the intent was "react when something happens," a webhook usually fits. Where it was "keep an eye on this channel," expect a gap.
- **GitHub access.** Install Jiro's GitHub App and select repositories [6]. The Claude GitHub App stays installed for Tag during the pilot.
- **Repo hooks and `.mcp.json`.** Tag skips these [7]. Teams that worked around that by moving setup elsewhere can now put it in the org setup script [8]. Verify behavior on a real task rather than assuming it.
- **Spend limits.** Not carried over, and mostly unnecessary on a flat plan. The subscription's own usage limits still apply.

Slack thread history is unaffected. Old Tag threads remain readable where they are.

## Day 1: setup

Plan for one sitting. Steps in order:

- **1. Open a trial account.** It lasts a month and asks for no card [9].
- **2. Connect GitHub.** Install the GitHub App; choose all repositories or a selected set. For the pilot, select only the repos in scope.
- **3. Connect Slack.** Add Jiro to the workspace and invite it to the new pilot channel only.
- **4. Connect a model login.** For Claude, run `claude setup-token` on a local machine first; it issues a one-year token linked to the Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan [10]. Connect that token in Jiro. Other routes: Codex sign-in via OAuth, raw keys from OpenAI or Anthropic, or, for the Cursor harness only, a Cursor key [11].
- **5. Draft the org setup script.** Have it install the dependencies, CLIs and services every task needs [8]. Keep it short at first.
- **6. Add shared context.** Move the copied Tag skills into a skillset. Optionally add Jiro's own engineering skills with `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`.
- **7. Run a first task.** A small documentation fix in a familiar repo. Confirm a pull request arrives [12] and that CI runs on it.

If step 7 fails, fix the setup script before routing real work. Most early failures are missing dependencies.

## Routing rule for the pilot

Comparable tasks go to both tools, alternately. Odd-numbered tickets to Tag, even-numbered to Jiro, or any equally boring rule. Hand-picking which tool gets the "easy" ticket ruins the data.

Once a week, give the same task to both. One paired comparison per week is enough. More than that wastes reviewer time.

## Week one: low-risk work

The first week tests setup and review flow, not raw capability.

- Fill a documentation gap someone has complained about twice.
- Add missing tests around a module with low coverage.
- Clean up dead code or duplicated helpers flagged in a recent review.
- Close two or three small tickets that have sat in the backlog for a month.
- Take one on-call fix, ideally started from a webhook from your CI or alerting [5].

Expect friction in the first two days. Setup scripts rarely survive first contact with a real monorepo.

## Week two: real work and measurement

Move to tickets the team would have done anyway. Include at least one task that needs an integration such as Linear or Jira, and one scheduled job.

Record the following per task, in a shared sheet, for both tools:

- Time from request to first pull request.
- Review rounds before merge, or "abandoned."
- Whether the change matched what a teammate would have written, rated by the reviewer.
- Model usage consumed, from the Claude Tag spend dashboard and from the subscription's usage page.

Jiro is designed to question a weak plan and raise concerns early. Log those interruptions too. Some are useful; some are noise, and the ratio matters.

## What the team gives up

Leaving Tag has real costs. They should be written down before the decision, not after.

- **Shared visibility.** Tag lets anyone in a channel tag @Claude and the whole channel sees the reply [13]. Jiro also works in Slack threads [14], but teams used to Tag's channel culture will need to rebuild the habit.
- **Proactive watches.** Tag's channel watches and PR subscriptions [15] have no documented counterpart.
- **GitLab.** Tag supports GitLab through a service-account token [16]. Jiro's documented path is GitHub.
- **Self-hosted runners.** Tag can run inside the company network [17]. Jiro runs in Nori's cloud, one tenant per org [18].
- **One fewer vendor.** Tag is part of the Anthropic contract. Jiro adds a second supplier.

## Cost comparison

Claude Tag charges channel work by usage against an organization balance [19], and Team plans must prepay before Claude responds [20]. Record the two-week Tag spend directly from the admin dashboard.

Jiro is flat: Developer $99 a month, Team $250 a month with five shared runtimes [9]. Model tokens come from the team's own subscription with no added markup [21]. If a Max login hits its cap, overflow is billed as extra usage at standard API pricing [22], so record that line too.

Compare like for like: Tag spend plus Claude seats, against Jiro plan plus the same seats plus any extra usage.

## Day 14: the decision

Three outcomes are acceptable. Adopt Jiro and retire the Tag channel. Keep Tag and let the Jiro trial lapse; there is no card on file, so nothing converts. Or keep both, with a written rule about which work goes where.

The fourth outcome, "keep both indefinitely with no rule," is not acceptable. It doubles the review surface.

For a wider view of the field before deciding, the [Claude Tag alternatives](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/claude-tag) list covers six other options.

## FAQ

### Can Claude Tag and Jiro run in the same Slack workspace?

Yes. Keep them in separate channels during the pilot so results stay attributable.

### Do I need a Claude Team plan to use Jiro?

No. Any Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan works through `claude setup-token` [10], and ChatGPT logins or API keys work too [11].

### Will our Claude Tag skills work in Jiro?

Not automatically. Copy them into an org skillset; it is then translated into each agent's instruction file [2].

### What happens to the trial if we decide against Jiro?

It ends after 30 days. No card was collected, so nothing is charged [9].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Codex Cloud to Jiro (2026): What Changes on the Bill

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Codex cloud to Jiro?**
>
> You do not have to stop using Codex. Open a trial, add Jiro's GitHub App to your repos, connect Slack, then sign Jiro's Codex harness in with your existing ChatGPT login through Codex OAuth or with an OpenAI API key. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Your AGENTS.md stays in the repo and Codex reads it as before; the bill gains one flat line, $99 or $250 a month, and nothing else.

## Here's what changes on the bill

Short version first.

- **ChatGPT subscription:** unchanged. Codex cloud lives inside ChatGPT from Plus at $20, with Business at $25 per user [1]. Keep it. Jiro signs in to it.
- **New line:** either $99 monthly (Developer: a single seat, three persistent runtimes at most) or $250 monthly (Team: several seats, five runtimes in common) [2].
- **Token markup:** zero [3]. If you use an OpenAI API key instead, OpenAI bills you directly at its rates.
- **Idle cost:** runtimes go to sleep when nobody is using them and wake on demand [4].
- **Trial:** thirty days, five runtimes, no card [4].

That is the whole delta. The rest of this memo explains what you get for it, and what you lose.

## Why the bill is worth changing

Three reasons, in order of how often teams cite them to us.

First, model independence. Codex cloud is an OpenAI-models product, and cloud tasks are reserved for ChatGPT plan holders, not bare API keys [5]. Inside Jiro, Codex accepts either Codex OAuth or an OpenAI API key, and the same environment can run Claude Code or Cursor tomorrow [6] [7]. Switching models becomes a setting rather than a purchase order.

Second, unattended work. Jiro takes cron schedules, one-off reminders and webhooks [8], so a nightly test-gap sweep or a webhook from your alerting can start a task while everyone sleeps.

Third, the review step. In Codex cloud a person reviews the diff and then commits or opens the pull request [9]. Jiro hands back the pull request itself [10]. Fewer clicks; same scrutiny.

## Three sample bills

Illustrative, using list prices from the cited pages.

- **Solo engineer on ChatGPT Plus.** Before: $20 [1]. After: $20 plus $99 on Developer. Total $119.
- **Five engineers on ChatGPT Business.** Before: $125. After: $125 plus $250 on Team. Total $375, for five shared runtimes the whole group can use from Slack.
- **Twelve engineers, half on Claude, half on ChatGPT.** Before: two separate agent tools, likely. After: both subscriptions unchanged, one Jiro Team plan at $250 running Codex for some people and Claude Code for others.

The third case is where the numbers usually work out best. Two tools become one, and the team stops arguing about which vendor to standardize on.

One caveat. Five runtimes is a ceiling on concurrent sessions for Team, so a large group running many tasks at once will feel it.

## What carries over

AGENTS.md, entirely. It is a file in your repository, so Jiro's Codex harness reads it exactly as Codex cloud did. No export, no conversion.

Rules you want across every repo, or for Claude Code too, go into a Jiro skillset; Jiro writes each skillset out in the format a given harness reads, so Claude Code receives a CLAUDE.md while Codex keeps getting AGENTS.md [11]. Codex cloud environment settings do not carry over automatically. Rewrite the install steps as Jiro's org setup script, which prepares every session's environment the same way [12].

## Migration steps

- **Step 1.** Open the Jiro trial. Free for 30 days.
- **Step 2.** Add the GitHub App; grant it only the repositories in scope for now [13].
- **Step 3.** Connect your Slack workspace, so requests and replies live in team threads [14] [15].
- **Step 4.** Connect Codex. Sign in through Codex OAuth with the ChatGPT account you already pay for, or paste an OpenAI API key.
- **Step 5.** Optional, for Claude Code as well: on your own computer, run `claude setup-token` to generate a twelve-month token linked to your Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan [16], then add it to Jiro. Cursor needs a Cursor API key instead [6].
- **Step 6.** Port your Codex environment setup into the org setup script.
- **Step 7.** Post the first task in Slack. Keep it small.

Optional but cheap: run `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` to add Jiro's engineering skills.

## First-week budget of work

Spend the trial on tasks whose value you can price.

- Docs for one under-documented service. Cost of not doing it: every onboarding.
- Test coverage on the three files with the most recent bug fixes.
- A slop sweep: unused exports, duplicated utilities, stale TODOs.
- Two small tickets from the backlog that nobody has picked up in a month.
- One on-call fix, if production offers you one.

Count merged pull requests and reviewer minutes per merge. Those two numbers justify the line item or they do not.

## What you give up

Leaving Codex cloud entirely costs you some things. Weigh them.

- Starting tasks from ChatGPT's web, mobile and desktop apps, the IDE extension, and Linear [17].
- Codex Code Review, plus the Linear and GitHub hooks. All three sit on legacy infrastructure OpenAI means to retire, so this loss may arrive regardless [18].
- An agent that costs nothing extra on top of ChatGPT. Jiro is a separate fee.

Note the word "entirely". Most teams keep ChatGPT anyway.

## Pilot: run both for a month

Keep Codex cloud for anything started from ChatGPT; route Slack requests and scheduled work to Jiro. Assign each repository to one tool during the pilot to avoid conflicting branches. At month end, compare merged pull requests per dollar and how often reviewers sent work back.

If the numbers do not justify $99 or $250, cancel. The trial asks for no card, so there is nothing to claw back.

For the wider field, see the [Codex cloud alternatives ranking](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/codex-cloud).

## FAQ

### Can I keep using Codex after switching to Jiro?

Yes. Codex is one of Jiro's three harnesses, and it signs in with Codex OAuth or an OpenAI API key [6].

### Will my AGENTS.md still work?

Yes. It lives in the repository, and Codex in Jiro reads it unchanged.

### Do I still need a ChatGPT plan?

Only if you want Jiro's Codex to bill against it via Codex OAuth. With an OpenAI API key you pay OpenAI per token instead, at its standard rates, with no Jiro markup [3].

### Is Jiro cheaper than Codex cloud?

No. Codex cloud comes bundled with ChatGPT [1], and Jiro adds $99 or $250 a month [2]. The fee buys model choice, Slack and scheduled work, and pull requests returned for review.

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from GitHub Copilot Coding Agent to Jiro (2026): A Three-Phase Admin Rollout

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from GitHub Copilot coding agent to Jiro?**
>
> Roll out in three phases (one pilot repository, then one team, then the organization) and leave Copilot enabled until each phase meets its exit criteria. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Start the free trial, scope its GitHub App to the pilot repository, connect Slack and your Claude or ChatGPT credentials, then restate copilot-instructions.md as a skillset that Nori can render back into Copilot's format for as long as you run both.

## Scope of this plan

This is written for the person who owns GitHub organization settings. It assumes a team small enough that one administrator can run the rollout, roughly five to twenty engineers, and an existing Anthropic or OpenAI plan that Jiro will run on.

Budget four weeks. Most of that is waiting for real tasks to accumulate, not configuration.

## Inventory: what migrates, what is rebuilt, what stays

**Instructions migrate, by hand.** Nori skillsets are authored once and emitted in each agent's native format, so one source yields copilot-instructions.md for GitHub's agent, a CLAUDE.md file and an AGENTS.md file elsewhere [1]. Nothing imports `.github/copilot-instructions.md` automatically, so plan an hour to split it by topic: repository-wide rules into AGENTS.md, and narrower procedures (test conventions, release steps, migration rules) into individual skills. Because the skillset can emit copilot-instructions.md again, Copilot keeps reading the same guidance during the overlap.

**Environment setup is rebuilt.** Whatever you configured for Copilot's Actions runner [2] does not transfer. Restate it as an org setup script, which prepares every Jiro environment with your dependencies [3].

**Engineering defaults can be added.** Jiro's own engineering skills install with `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` and sit beside yours.

**History stays behind.** Copilot sessions, issue assignments and draft PRs remain in GitHub, where they belong.

## Phase 0: administrator setup, day one

Complete these in order. Each step has one owner: you.

- **Step 1. Begin the 30-day trial.** No card is requested [4].
- **Step 2. Install the GitHub App on the pilot repository only.** Choose a selected set rather than all repositories [5]; you will widen it in phase two.
- **Step 3. Connect Slack** and invite Jiro to the pilot team's channel [6].
- **Step 4. Connect model credentials.** On your own laptop, open a terminal, run `claude setup-token` and finish the browser sign-in; the command prints a token that stays valid for a year and is bound to the Claude plan you signed in with [7]. Paste that into Jiro. Alternatives, if your organization prefers them: Codex OAuth, API keys from either vendor, or a Cursor key [8].
- **Step 5. Write the org setup script** from the runner configuration you inventoried above.
- **Step 6. Assign the first task** in the Slack channel, and read the transcript afterwards.

Exit criterion: one pull request opened by Jiro, reviewed and merged by a human.

## Phase 1: a single pilot repository, week one

Choose a repository with good tests and an owner who will review promptly. Then hand Jiro the work your team keeps deferring.

- **Monday:** have Jiro reconcile the README and onboarding docs with current behavior.
- **Tuesday:** find the three least-tested modules and propose tests for each.
- **Wednesday:** clean up one area of slop, for instance stale feature flags or a helper copied into four files.
- **Thursday:** two small tickets from the backlog, assigned in Slack.
- **Friday:** point a webhook from your CI or alerting at Jiro [9] and let it take the next on-call fix.

Watch how it behaves, not only what it ships. A good pilot shows Jiro questioning a vague ticket before writing code.

Exit criteria: at least five merged pull requests, no review escalations, and reviewers willing to continue.

## Phase 2: one team, weeks two and three

Widen the GitHub App selection to the team's repositories. Move to the Team plan so several engineers share five runtimes [4]; runtimes sleep when nobody is using them [10].

This is also when the integrations go in. Admins connect MCP servers from the catalog once for every session [11], and tools such as Linear, Jira, Notion or Stripe become available to Jiro while it works [12]. Add one recurring job on a cron schedule, for example a weekly documentation pass.

Exit criterion: the team prefers Jiro for at least one category of work.

## Phase 3: the organization, week four onward

Extend the GitHub App to all repositories, or to every repository a policy allows. Hand your security reviewer two facts: the broker serving your organization is single-tenant, on its own subdomain [13], and every session and action is logged and searchable [14].

Then decide on Copilot seats. Some teams keep them for IDE completion; others retire them.

## Permissions and review policy

Leave review policy exactly as it is. Copilot's agent opens drafts on its own branch and cannot approve or merge [15]; Jiro returns a pull request, commit or comment for your team to review [16], and your existing branch protection and required reviewers decide what merges. Do not loosen either during the pilot.

Scope is the other lever. Keep the GitHub App on a selected set until phase three.

## What leaving Copilot costs you

Be honest about the trade. Copilot starts tasks from GitHub issues, pull requests, Mobile, IDEs, the CLI, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Linear, Jira and Azure Boards [17], and Jiro does not take work from Teams or Boards. You also lose the single GitHub invoice and the runner model your platform team already understands.

What you gain is ownership of the model contract.

## Cost: seats and credits against flat runtimes

Copilot Business is $19 per user and Enterprise $39 [18], so ten engineers on Business pay $190 a month before usage, which since June 2026 is metered in AI Credits by token [19]. Jiro's Team plan is $250 a month flat, and Developer is $99 for one user [4].

The comparison is not complete without models. With Jiro you pay Anthropic or OpenAI directly (Claude Max, for instance, costs each engineer $100 or $200 monthly [20]) and Nori adds no token markup [21]. If those subscriptions already exist, the marginal cost is the plan alone.

## Running both through the pilot

Nothing forces a cutover date. Copilot's agent can keep taking issue assignments while Jiro takes Slack requests, and the shared skillset keeps both reading the same rules. Compare them on the same kind of task for a fortnight, then decide.

For the full field of options, see the [Copilot coding agent alternatives](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/copilot-coding-agent) ranking.

## FAQ

### Does Jiro import copilot-instructions.md automatically?

No. You move its contents into a skillset or AGENTS.md by hand; afterwards Nori can render that skillset back into copilot-instructions.md, alongside CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md [1].

### Can we limit Jiro to specific repositories?

Yes. The GitHub App installs on all repositories or on a set you select [5], which is how the pilot phase is scoped.

### Can Jiro use our Claude Team or Enterprise plan?

Yes. Someone on that plan mints a token locally with `claude setup-token` [7], then connect it in Jiro; Anthropic API keys and Claude OAuth also work [8].

### Should we cancel Copilot before the pilot ends?

No. Run both until phase two's exit criterion is met; some organizations keep Copilot seats for editor completion permanently.

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Cursor to Jiro (2026): Every Workflow, Before and After

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Cursor to Jiro?**
>
> Keep Cursor as your editor, move cloud-agent work to Jiro one workflow at a time, and copy your Cursor rules into AGENTS.md and skills by hand. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Setup takes an afternoon: start the trial, install the GitHub App, connect Slack, connect a Claude token from `claude setup-token` (or Codex, or a Cursor API key if you want Cursor's agent inside Jiro), write an org setup script, then hand over one real ticket.

## You don't have to leave Cursor

Most people who switch keep the editor open all day. What moves is the background work, the tasks you used to fire off to Cursor's Cloud Agents [1]. And if you like Cursor's agent itself, Jiro can run it: Cursor is one of the three harnesses alongside Claude Code and Codex [2], on a Cursor API key you supply [3].

So this guide is less a migration than a rearrangement. Here's each workflow, before and after.

## Workflow by workflow

**Starting a task.** Before: you opened the Cursor app, the web or iOS, or tagged Cursor in Slack, and the agent went off on its own [4]. After: you mention Jiro in a Slack thread, the web chat, Discord or a terminal [5] [6], your teammates see the thread, and Jiro may push back on the ticket first if something looks off.

**Paying for models.** Before: Premium ($30 monthly) was the entry ticket for cloud agents, with third-party model usage draining prepaid credit at list API rates [7], since custom keys only cover chat [8]. After: Claude Code and Codex bill against an Anthropic or OpenAI plan that's already on the company card, and Nori adds zero markup on tokens [9].

**Project rules.** Before: conventions lived in Cursor rules files. After: they live in AGENTS.md and skills, packaged as a skillset that Nori translates into CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or copilot-instructions.md depending on the agent [10]. Cursor's format is not in that list, so this part is a copy-and-edit job (details below).

**The environment.** Before: Cursor provisioned a full dev environment in its cloud or on a self-hosted worker [11]. After: every Jiro conversation gets its own cloud machine [12], prepared by one org setup script that installs your dependencies [13].

**Recurring chores.** Before: you remembered to ask. After: a cron schedule or a webhook starts the job [14], whether that's a Monday docs pass or the alert that fires at 2 a.m.

**What comes back.** Before: a polished PR, often with a screen recording attached [15]. After: a reviewable PR, a commit or a comment, back in the thread [16]. Fewer movies. More discussion in the thread.

## Porting Cursor rules, without pretending

There's no importer. Here is the manual route, which takes most teams under an hour.

- Open each rules file and sort its content into two piles: rules that apply everywhere, and procedures that apply to one kind of task.
- Put the everywhere rules in an AGENTS.md at the repository root.
- Turn each procedure (how to add a migration, how to cut a release, which test runner to use) into its own skill.
- Bundle the skills into a skillset so every Jiro session gets them. Add Jiro's own engineering skills too, via `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` in a terminal.
- Leave your original rules files where they are. Your editor still reads them.

Expect drift between the two copies for a while. Pick one as the source of truth and say so in the file.

## Setup in six steps

- **1. Trial.** Sign up; 30 days free, no card [17].
- **2. GitHub.** Install the GitHub App and choose which repositories Jiro can touch [18].
- **3. Slack.** Connect your workspace and invite Jiro into a channel.
- **4. Models.** For Claude, run `claude setup-token` on your laptop, sign in when the browser opens, and copy the resulting token, which is tied to your paid Claude plan and lasts a year [19]; paste it into Jiro. Codex users sign in through OAuth or paste an OpenAI key instead. For Cursor's agent, paste a Cursor API key.
- **5. Setup script.** Write the org script that installs your toolchain, so each machine boots ready.
- **6. First task.** Give it something small and real, then read the whole transcript.

## Your first week

Start with work Cursor's agent never got asked to do, because nobody had the time.

- Day one: a docs refresh, starting with whatever the README gets wrong.
- Day two: find untested branches in one important module and cover them.
- Day three: a slop sweep, removing dead code and stale feature flags in one directory.
- Day four: two small tickets you'd normally leave for a quiet Friday.
- Day five: wire a webhook from your alerting and hand Jiro the next on-call fix.

By Friday you'll know whether the push-back is useful or annoying. Usually it's both, at first.

## What you give up

Some real things. Cursor works with GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps repositories and takes requests from Microsoft Teams, Linear and an API [4]; Jiro connects to code through GitHub. The screenshot-and-video PRs are excellent, and Jiro doesn't produce them. Self-hosted workers are also a Cursor feature [11].

Where one of those matters to your team, leave that workflow with Cursor.

## What it costs

Before: at least $30 a month for Premium, plus model usage at API list price [7]. After: $99 monthly on Developer buys a single user three persistent runtimes, or $250 monthly on Team buys five shared ones for everybody [17]. Model costs go to Anthropic or OpenAI directly, often on a Claude Max plan at $100 or $200 a month you may already own [20].

For a team of six with Claude plans already paid, the after column is one flat bill.

## Running both during the pilot

This is the easy part. Keep Cursor for editing, keep its cloud agents for anything on GitLab or with a video-heavy review, and send everything Slack-shaped to Jiro. If you want an apples-to-apples test, run the same ticket through Cursor's agent inside Jiro and through Claude Code inside Jiro, then compare the diffs.

Still weighing options? The [Cursor background agents alternatives](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/cursor-background-agents) page ranks the rest of the field.

## FAQ

### Can I keep using Cursor's agent after switching?

Yes. Jiro runs the Cursor harness on your Cursor API key [3].

### Do my Cursor rules carry over automatically?

No. Copy them into AGENTS.md and skills by hand; Nori's translation covers CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and copilot-instructions.md, not Cursor's rule files [10].

### Do I need to cancel my Cursor plan?

Not necessarily. Many teams keep it for the editor. If you're on a legacy Pro, Pro+ or Teams plan, note that moving to Cursor's new plans is optional but permanent [21].

### How do I use my Claude subscription with Jiro?

On your laptop, `claude setup-token` creates a token for your Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan [19], then connect it in Jiro.

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

9. Nori's comparison table lists any model on your own keys with flat pricing and zero token markup. Source: https://noriagentic.com/#compare (checked 2026-10-19)
10. A Nori skillset is written once and translated into each agent's own files: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, copilot-instructions.md for GitHub Copilot and AGENTS.md for most others. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/skillsets/concepts/translation-and-agents (checked 2026-10-19)
11. Cursor cloud agents run in isolated cloud VMs with full development environments, or on self-hosted workers while Cursor runs the agent loop. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent.md (checked 2026-10-16)
12. In Nori, one claimed machine serves one active session within the organization's fleet. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/resources/faq#is-each-session-isolated (checked 2026-10-19)
13. A Nori organization can define a setup script that installs dependencies and prepares every session's environment. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/start/what-can-nori-do#give-agents-a-real-working-environment (checked 2026-10-19)
14. Nori cron triggers run recurring jobs, reminders run once at a future time, and webhooks react to external events. Source: https://docs.noriagentic.com/resources/faq#can-nori-run-tasks-without-a-person-online (checked 2026-10-19)
15. Cursor cloud agents produce merge-ready PRs with screenshots, videos and logs, and open a PR in each repo they touch. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent.md (checked 2026-10-16)
16. Nori agents can return a pull request, commit, comment or completed task for you to review, merge or send back. Source: https://noriagentic.com/#faq (checked 2026-10-19)

20. Claude Max costs $100 a month for 5x the Pro plan's per-session usage or $200 a month for 20x, with limits that reset every five hours plus a weekly limit. Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11049741-what-is-the-max-plan (checked 2026-10-17)
21. Customers on Cursor's legacy Pro, Pro+ and Teams plans can keep them; switching to the new plans is optional but permanent. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/account/pricing/legacy-cursor-plans.md (checked 2026-10-16)

# Switching from Devin to Jiro (2026): Setup Steps and a First-Week Plan

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Devin to Jiro?**
>
> Start Jiro's free 30-day trial, install the GitHub App on the repositories Devin was using, connect Slack, sign in with your Claude plan through `claude setup-token` (or connect Codex or Cursor), add an org setup script, and give it a first small task. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Devin Knowledge and playbooks do not import automatically, so plan an hour to copy the useful ones into a skillset or AGENTS.md.

## Before we start: what this page is

This is an illustrative plan, written the way a small team would actually run the move. It is not a customer story. Think of it as the notes we would want in front of us if we were the ones leaving Devin on a Monday.

The short version? Most of what matters lives in your repos, and that comes with you. The rest is a bit of copying.

## What carries over, and what we copied by hand

Repositories carry over trivially, since Jiro installs as a GitHub App and you pick all repos or a chosen set. [1] Slack carries over too; it is the same workspace with a different bot to mention.

Devin's Knowledge entries and playbooks are another matter. There is no importer. We would export the ones the team still trusts and paste them into a Nori skillset, which Jiro then writes out as CLAUDE.md for Claude Code or AGENTS.md for Codex and most others. [2] [3] If your repos already have a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, the agent reads it as usual, so that part needs nothing.

The usual advice for this kind of cleanup: do not copy everything. Half of any Knowledge base is notes about a bug fixed in March.

Automations need rebuilding. Scheduled Devin sessions map onto Jiro cron triggers, and webhook ones onto Jiro webhooks. [4] [5] Sessions that Devin started from Linear or GitHub events have no direct equivalent in Jiro, so either point a webhook at Jiro or have someone mention it in Slack.

## Setup, in six steps

- **1. Open a trial account.** It lasts 30 days, asks for no card, and gives you five runtimes to play with. [6] [7]
- **2. Install the GitHub App** and select the repositories Devin had. [1]
- **3. Connect Slack** so the team can mention Jiro in channels and threads. [8] [9]
- **4. Sign in to a model.** Claude subscribers do this on their own laptop: we installed the Claude command line, ran `claude setup-token`, and copied the year-long token it printed, which is bound to whichever Claude plan the account holds. [10] Paste it into Jiro. On ChatGPT? Connect Codex OAuth or an OpenAI key. Cursor users bring their own Cursor key. [11]
- **5. Add an org setup script.** Install the toolchain, the package manager, the database client, whatever a new hire would install on day one. [12]
- **6. Hand it a first task** in Slack. Something small and checkable.

Optional but useful: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` puts Jiro's own engineering skills in place.

## The first week, day by day

**Monday:** setup, then one job. We would ask Jiro to read the main repo and report the three places where docs and code disagree most. It is a cheap way to see how it reads your codebase, and the output is a pull request against the README, which nobody minds reviewing.

**Tuesday:** test gaps. Pick a module everyone is slightly afraid of and ask for tests around its public behaviour, no refactors. Review hard. This is where you learn whether its taste matches yours.

**Wednesday:** slop cleanup. Every codebase that has had agents in it has some: duplicate helpers, dead flags, comments narrating the obvious. Ask Jiro to find and remove one category of it, and to say what it chose not to touch.

**Thursday:** small tickets. Three of them, from the bottom of the backlog, the kind that sit there for a quarter. Have three people each mention Jiro on one, so the team gets used to the thread workflow.

**Friday:** an on-call fix. Wire a webhook from your CI or alerting to Jiro, or just paste the alert into Slack, and let it propose the fix as a pull request. [5] [13] Then sit down and compare the week's PRs with what Devin produced on similar work.

By Friday you know. Either the reviews felt lighter or they did not.

## What we would give up by leaving Devin

Being honest about this is the whole point of a pilot. Devin covers Microsoft Teams, GitLab and Bitbucket, and Jiro does not today. [14] Jira is not a gap; Jiro connects to it as an integration. [15] Devin opens sessions directly from Linear and GitHub events. [4] Its PR maintenance is strong: stacked PRs, conflict fixes, replies to review comments. [16] And an Enterprise buyer can get a dedicated VPC, which Nori's hosting is not. [17]

If any of those is load-bearing for you, the move costs more than a week.

## What it costs, side by side

Jiro's Developer plan is $99 a month for one person and up to three persistent runtimes; Team is $250 a month for several people sharing five. [6] Tokens come out of the Anthropic or OpenAI plans already on your card, and Nori adds nothing to them. [18]

Devin's Teams plan has an $80 monthly minimum plus $40 a seat, and usage past the quota bills at API pricing. [19]

For a team of eight that already pays for Claude, the comparison is one runtime fee against a seat bill plus overage, and overage is where the money goes: we have seen heavy Devin use by eight people approach $4,000 a month. Without those subscriptions, add them to Jiro's side before you compare.

## Running both during the pilot

We would keep Devin on for the 30 days. Give each agent its own Slack channel so nobody tags the wrong bot, point both at the same repos, and split the week's tasks between them. Label the PRs. At the end, count merged versus closed, and ask reviewers which ones they would rather have read.

Then cancel one. Both if neither was worth it, frankly.

## FAQ

### Can Jiro import Devin Knowledge or playbooks?

Not automatically. Copy the entries worth keeping into a Nori skillset or an AGENTS.md file, and Jiro translates the skillset into each agent's own instruction file. [2]

### Do I have to use a Claude subscription?

No. Claude Code also takes an Anthropic API key, Codex takes an OpenAI key or Codex OAuth, and Cursor runs on a Cursor API key. [11]

### Why do I need to run claude setup-token myself?

Subscription sign-in happens on your own machine, where the command creates a long-lived token for your plan; Jiro's cloud machine then uses that token. [10]

### Can I set this up from my phone?

The setup lives in the cloud, and the Miravoice team did theirs from phones. [20] The `claude setup-token` step needs a computer with the Claude command line, though.

### Where can I compare other options first?

We ranked eight of them in our [Devin roundup](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/devin).

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Factory to Jiro (2026): Cutover and Rollback Runbook

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Factory to Jiro?**
>
> Run Jiro alongside Factory for one or two weeks: start the free trial, install the GitHub App on a few pilot repos, connect Slack, sign in with your Claude or ChatGPT plan, write an org setup script, then route small tickets to Jiro and compare. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Keep Factory live until the pilot passes, so rollback is just turning Jiro off.

## Scope

This runbook covers a team of roughly 5 to 20 engineers moving delegated coding work from Factory's Droids to Jiro. It assumes GitHub, Slack, and an existing Claude or ChatGPT subscription.

Out of scope: Factory Private installs. If you run Droids inside your VPC or an air-gapped network [1], stop here. Jiro is hosted and has no on-premises edition.

Estimated effort: one afternoon to set up. Two weeks of parallel running.

## Before you start

Complete every item. Do not begin cutover with open questions.

- **Inventory automations.** List each Factory automation you rely on, such as Ticket to PR or Error Triage [2]. Note what fires it and where its output goes.
- **Inventory intake.** Write down where Droid work starts today. Factory accepts delegations from Slack, Linear and Jira [3]; Jiro's entry points are chat (Slack, Discord, the web), the terminal, cron and webhooks [4]. Anything that depends on assigning a Linear or Jira ticket to the agent needs a new path.
- **Collect instructions.** Find every file of agent guidance: repo-level `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, plus any conventions you keep inside Factory. Repo files stay where they are. The rest gets copied by hand.
- **Pick pilot repos.** Two or three. One should be boring.
- **Confirm model access.** Every pilot user needs one of: a paid Claude seat, ChatGPT, an Anthropic or OpenAI key, or (Cursor harness only) a Cursor-issued key [5].
- **Name an owner.** One person writes the setup script and reads every pilot PR.

## What carries over

Instruction files committed to your repos come along untouched, because the harnesses Jiro runs read them natively: Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, Codex reads `AGENTS.md`.

Org-wide conventions should move into a Jiro skillset. Write it once; Nori renders the per-agent file for whichever harness runs, so Claude Code sees a `CLAUDE.md` while Codex sees an `AGENTS.md` [6]. Nothing imports from Factory automatically. Copy, then trim.

Automations get rebuilt. A nightly Error Triage becomes a cron trigger; a Ticket to PR flow becomes a webhook from your tracker or alerting, or a person pasting the link into Slack [7].

## Cutover

Execute in order. Each step lists its check.

1. **Open a trial account.** No payment details required; the clock runs 30 days [8]. Check: you can open web chat.
2. **Install the GitHub App.** Select only the pilot repos, not all repositories [9]. Check: in web chat, ask Jiro to list the files in one pilot repo.
3. **Connect Slack.** Create a channel such as `#jiro-pilot` and invite the bot. Check: a hello message gets a reply.
4. **Connect the model.** On your own laptop, run `claude setup-token`. Output: a token valid for twelve months, bound to the paid Claude plan you hold, whether that is Pro or Max or a Team or Enterprise seat [10]. Paste it into Jiro's Claude connection. Codex alternative: Codex OAuth, else an OpenAI key. Cursor alternative: a Cursor-issued API key [5]. Check: a one-line coding question in Slack gets a real answer.
5. **Write the org setup script.** Install runtimes, package managers and anything your tests need [11]. Check: ask Jiro to run the test suite on a pilot repo and report results. It should pass the same way it passes in CI.
6. **Write the skillset.** Move the conventions you collected into your org skillset [12]. Optional, for developers running agents locally as well: the command is `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`, run on their own laptops.
7. **Connect trackers.** Add Linear or Jira, and any MCP servers you need from the catalog [13] [14]. Check: Jiro can read a ticket you link.
8. **Send the first task.** Something small with an obvious right answer. Check: a pull request arrives for review [15].

Do not disable any Factory automation yet.

## First week

Feed the pilot real work, in rising order of risk.

- **Day 1.** Docs. Ask Jiro to diff the README against reality and correct whatever drifted.
- **Day 2.** Tests. Point it at a module with thin coverage and ask for the missing cases, not new features.
- **Day 3.** Cleanup. Hand it a directory full of agent slop and ask for the diff a careful teammate would leave behind.
- **Day 4.** Small tickets. Three of them, straight from the backlog, posted in the pilot channel.
- **Day 5.** On-call. Wire a webhook from CI or alerting, or schedule a cron job that checks a known flaky area each morning [7].

Log for each task: time to first PR, review rounds, and whether a reviewer had to rewrite anything. Do the same for Factory on comparable tickets. You want numbers, not vibes.

Expect pushback. Jiro will question tickets that look wrong. Record those too; they count.

## What you give up

Be honest about this before you commit.

- On-premises and air-gapped deployment through Factory Private [1].
- Delegating by assigning a Linear or Jira ticket directly to the agent [3].
- Packaged automation templates that open PRs with no prompt [2]. You rebuild these yourself.
- Factory's own model routing across vendors [16]. With Jiro you pick the harness and the plan.

What you gain, briefly: your own Claude or ChatGPT plan working in the cloud, where Factory only accepts your own keys in its CLI and desktop app [16], plus no token markup [17].

## Cost check

Compare list prices for a five-person team.

- Factory Teams: $60 a month plus $40 per seat, so $260 for five [18].
- Jiro Team: $250 monthly, five runtimes shared across the whole team [8].
- Solo: Factory Pro is $20 a month and Plus $100 [18]; Jiro Developer is $99 with up to three persistent runtimes, before your own model plan.

Jiro's price excludes model usage. You pay Anthropic or OpenAI directly, on plans many teams already hold. Heavy users may want Claude Max, at $100 or $200 a month [19]. Runtimes sleep when idle [20], so quiet weeks cost nothing extra.

## Running both

Keep Factory fully active during the pilot. Route by channel: Droid requests keep their current entry points, Jiro takes everything posted in the pilot channel. Never send the same ticket to both. Duplicate PRs waste reviewer time and spoil the comparison.

At the end of week two, review the log with the team. Pass criteria are yours to set, but write them down on day one.

## Rollback

If the pilot fails, reverse the cutover. Nothing on the Factory side changed, so there is nothing to restore.

1. Close or merge any open Jiro PRs.
2. Remove the Slack app from the pilot channel.
3. Uninstall the GitHub App or deselect the pilot repos.
4. Delete the Claude, OpenAI or Cursor credential from Jiro.
5. Let the trial lapse. No card was taken, so there is no charge.

Every session and action stays logged [21], which is useful for the post-pilot writeup either way.

Still comparing options? See the [Factory alternatives](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/factory) page.

## FAQ

### How long does a Factory to Jiro switch take?

Setup fits in an afternoon. Plan for two weeks of parallel running before you turn off any Factory automation.

### Do my Factory automations move over automatically?

No. Rebuild each one as a cron schedule or a webhook in Jiro [7]. Ticket-assignment flows from Linear or Jira need a new entry point, usually Slack.

### Can I use my Claude subscription instead of an API key?

Yes. Generate one with `claude setup-token` on your own computer; it lasts a year and is linked to your paid Claude plan [10]. Then paste it into Jiro.

### Does Jiro have an equivalent of Factory Private?

No. Jiro is hosted, with a single-tenant broker per organization [22]. If you need air-gapped or on-premises deployment, stay on Factory Private [1].

## Try Jiro

Start the 30-day free trial, no card needed: https://login.norisessions.com/?signup=1&entrypoint=jiro

Or install Jiro's engineering skills into your own agent: `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro`

# Switching from Jules to Jiro (2026): Quickstart, Gotchas and First Week

Updated 2026-10-19

> **How do I switch from Jules to Jiro?**
>
> Switching from Jules to Jiro takes six steps: start the free trial, install Nori's GitHub App, connect Slack, connect a Claude plan through claude setup-token (or Codex sign-in, an API key, or a Cursor key), write an org setup script, and send a first task. Jiro is a background coding agent by Nori. Repository instruction files stay where they are, Jules Scheduled Tasks become Jiro cron triggers, and the main things you leave behind are Gemini models and the jules issue label.

## Before you start

Have three things ready.

- Admin rights on the GitHub org.
- Permission to add an app to Slack.
- A Claude or ChatGPT plan, or an API key. Jiro doesn't run Gemini, so your Google AI subscription won't carry over [1].

Budget about an hour for setup. Then a week of small tasks.

## Quickstart

1. **Start the trial.** Thirty days free, no card required [2].
2. **Install the GitHub App.** Choose all repos or just the pilot ones [3].
3. **Connect Slack.** Requests will mostly come from there [4].
4. **Mint a Claude token.** Laptop, terminal, `claude setup-token`. Copy what it prints. That string is valid twelve months and draws on your paid Claude seat, be it Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise [5].
5. **Connect it in Jiro.** Paste the token. ChatGPT shop? Use the Codex login flow, or an OpenAI key. Cursor shop? Bring a Cursor key [6].
6. **Script the environment.** Put install commands, language versions and service setup here so every environment boots ready [7].
7. **Send a first task.** Mention @Jiro in a channel with something tiny. Review the PR [8].
8. **Optional: install Jiro's skills.** Run `npx nori-skillsets install public/jiro` for its engineering conventions.

## Port what you had

Mostly copy-paste.

- **Instruction files.** Leave AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md in the repo. For rules that should apply across repos, write a Nori skillset once and let Nori emit each harness's native file, whether that's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md [9].
- **Environment setup.** Jules gave you a stock VM with common toolchains and Docker [10]. If you added commands on top, move them into the setup script from step 6.
- **Scheduled Tasks.** Recreate each one as a Jiro cron trigger [11] [12].
- **API or CLI automations.** Rewire anything that called Jules to send a webhook to Jiro instead [12].
- **Google tools.** Connect Drive, Sheets or Gmail if tasks need them [13].

## Gotchas

- **No Gemini.** Jiro runs Claude Code, Codex or Cursor [14]. Prompts tuned for Gemini may need a nudge.
- **No issue label.** Jules picks up GitHub issues labelled jules [15]. Jiro doesn't watch labels. Paste the issue link into Slack instead, or wire a webhook.
- **PRs arrive, not drafts you publish.** In Jules you chose between Publish branch and Publish PR [16]. Jiro returns its work as a pull request, commit or comment for review [8], so set up branch protection if you haven't.
- **Model limits move.** Daily task caps go away [17], but your Claude or ChatGPT plan's own usage limits now apply.
- **Token expiry.** That setup token lasts a year. Put a reminder in the calendar.
- **Check the script first.** If an early task fails strangely, a missing install step in the setup script is the usual suspect.
- **Concurrency is different.** Jules counted concurrent tasks per tier: 3, 15 or 60 [17]. Jiro counts runtimes instead, and they sleep when idle [18].
- **One conversation, one machine.** Each active session gets its own [19]. Parallel threads mean parallel runtimes, and Developer includes three.

## First week

1. Day one: fix stale docs in the main README.
2. Day two: add missing tests for one module.
3. Day three: ask Jiro where the codebase has accumulated slop, and read the list before approving any cleanup.
4. Day four: hand over a small ticket from the backlog.
5. Day five: route one boring on-call fix to it.

Write each request the way you'd write a ticket for a new teammate: the goal, the file or module, how you'll judge it done. Expect questions back. Jiro is supposed to push on vague asks.

Keep tasks reviewable in a few minutes. Grow scope only after the PRs look like ones your team would have written.

## What you lose

- Gemini.
- The free tier, which gave fifteen tasks a day at no cost [17].
- Starting work straight from a GitHub label.
- Cheap single-person pricing bundled into a Google AI plan [20].

What you get in return is a team agent rather than a personal one: shared Slack threads [21], shared org context, and several harnesses behind one name.

## Cost check

- Jules: $0 on the free tier, $19.99/month via AI Pro, $99.99+/month via AI Ultra [20].
- Jiro Developer: $99 a month, one user, three persistent runtimes.
- Jiro Team: $250 a month, several users, five shared runtimes [2].
- Plus a model plan for every engineer: with Jiro, each person still needs their own Claude or ChatGPT plan, or an API key [6]. Claude Max sits at $100 or $200 monthly, depending on the multiplier [22].

Per person, Jules is cheaper. Per team, compare against what you'd spend putting every engineer on a paid Google AI plan instead of sharing one Jiro workspace, and remember Nori charges no markup on the model side [23].

## Run both for two weeks

Nothing stops you. Keep Jules for personal experiments. Route team chores to Jiro. Compare merged PRs and review time at the end.

Still deciding? Read the [Jules alternatives roundup](https://jiro.bot/alternatives/jules).

## FAQ

### Can Jiro use my Google AI Pro subscription?

No. Jiro runs on Claude or ChatGPT plans, API keys, or a Cursor key, not Gemini.

### Do my Jules Scheduled Tasks transfer automatically?

No. Recreate each one as a cron trigger in Jiro. It's a few minutes per task.

### Does Jiro work if our company uses Google Workspace?

Yes. Jiro's plans aren't tied to a Google account at all, and Drive, Sheets and Gmail are available as integrations.

### How fast can we be up and running?

About an hour to a first pull request, if your setup script is simple.
